💡 Key Takeaways
  • iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair.
  • Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.
  • Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

Industry observers note that iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

It has been revealed that percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%.

Percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%.

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

GTA 6’s Worst Feature Needs to Be Patched ASAP

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here.
  • In the early hours of the game, Jason doesn't have a bank account.
  • Recent findings suggest that at first, I generously assumed this was some kind of artistic flourish.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here. And somehow, miraculously, it's living up to the impossible level of hype surrounding it. Rockstar's game is a staggering technological and artistic achievement in countless ways. The world of Leonida is vast and intricate, and the emergent gameplay enabled by hundreds of unique NPCs is truly astonishing. But there's one thing about GTA 6 I find absolutely infuriating so far, and it's extremely minor: depositing and withdrawing money from Jason's stash box and ATMs is a total pain in the ass.

In the early hours of the game, Jason doesn't have a bank account. (He later tells Lucia he doesn't want to be "in the system.") So while he's making a living doing odd jobs and waiting for Lucia to be released from prison, he's keeping money under the floorboards in his bedroom. In order to select the amount you want to deposit or withdraw from the stash box, you press left or right on the d-pad. It takes forever for the numbers to tick up or down — until suddenly it doesn't, and you've whizzed far past the figure you wanted to input. The sensitivity of the counter is totally out of whack, going from a trickle to a fire hose instantaneously. I figured I was missing something — surely it should not be this difficult to wrangle the stash box?

Recent findings suggest that at first, I generously assumed this was some kind of artistic flourish. Jason isn't counting the cash he places in the stash by hand every time; he's just eyeballing it. Then, about halfway through Chapter 1, you get access to the BuckMe app, essentially a bank account for people with terrible credit like Jason and Lucia. In addition to keeping cash at home, you can now deposit your ill-gotten gains at ATMs throughout Leonida. (Having a BuckMe account also allows you to make more expensive purchases at the gun store.) I assumed my days of wrangling that horrible slider were over. Surely the ATM would feature a numerical keypad, and I could just enter the amount I wanted to deposit or withdraw. After all, a similar interface appears elsewhere in the game, for door codes and lockboxes. Nope! For no discernible reason, ATMs also use the same clunky, left-to-right scrolling interface as the stash box.

Perhaps the intent here is to encourage you to put all your money in your BuckMe and Family Savings account as soon as the option becomes available. But I enjoy having a few hundred dollars of "fuck around money​​​​​​​" for buying snacks or car repairs. Yes, you can use the app for most stuff, but I really hate the idea of having to schlep​​​​​​​ back to the house or find an ATM to get cash. I can't imagine this would be difficult for Rockstar to fix, and I would even tolerate it for the stash box if I must. But there is literally no excuse for an ATM to work this way in a video game in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that I'm not the only one who has beef with this mechanic. Plenty of folks on Reddit have noticed it too. "Ok I’m not the only one I was hoping there was a way to input the exact numbers and I haven’t found it yet but guess not," wrote one user. "Little bit more, little bit more, little bit more, ok and stop.... Fuck, way too much," wrote another.

The horrible banking interface does not appear to have slowed GTA 6's ascent to cultural dominance. The game sold more than 32 million copies during the run-up to release and has already made $3.79 billion in revenue, according to Rockstar Games. GTA 6 is available now on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X.

Latest Update: 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (489 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways.
  • Industry observers note that as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords.
  • You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that these so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

Industry observers note that as McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

In a recent development, unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

According to recent reports, next, audit accounts you've created using single sign-on, such as Google, Apple, or Facebook. For Google, this is under Account Settings > Linked apps. For Apple, go to System Settings > [Your Name] > Sign in with Apple on your Mac (or the same path in the Settings app on iOS). On Facebook, this is under Settings & privacy > Apps and websites. Disconnecting these accounts won't automatically delete them, but you can add them to the list to take action. Finally, you can search your email(s) on HaveIBeenPwned and username(s) on IDCrawl or WhatsMyName to find dormant accounts.

According to recent reports, once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Well, here we are: the end of the year. The days are shorter, the nights are longer, and our bank accounts are getting smaller. You know why: the holidays are upon us, which means we all have to spend money like the good little consumers we are. The official unofficial launch of the holiday season always begins on Black Friday, that day after Thanksgiving where we wake up hungover from eating too much and start looking for major beautiful deals.

If you're a horror movie fan, I've thrown together a little list of five great Black Friday deals on horror movies, all of which are under $20! That's not bad, especially these days, when everything is outrageously expensive. So if you're a physical media collector and looking for something spooky to drop a few bucks on, keep reading.

Danny Boyle's "28 Years Later" returned to the post-apocalyptic franchise he began with "28 Days Later," and he scored a major box office hit in the process. Unfortunately, "28 Years Later" was meant to be the first of a new trilogy, and the second movie, this year's "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple," wasn't a hit at all. As a result, the fate of the third and final movie in this new franchise is at the moment uncertain.

Which is a damn shame, because "The Bone Temple" absolutely rules. In fact, I think it's better than "28 Years Later." Ralph Fiennes returns as Dr. Ian Kelson, seemingly one of the last good men in a post-apocalyptic landscape overrun by rage-infected zombies and murderous groups of scavengers. This time, Dr. Kelson comes face to face with the deranged Jimmy Crystal (Jack O'Connell), all while trying to find a cure for that pesky rage virus.

According to recent reports, "Evil Dead Burn" is the latest entry in the long-running franchise, and it did something no previous "Evil Dead" film did before: it made some fans think the movie was just a little too nasty. The franchise has become known for its over-the-top gore, but Sébastien Vaniček's film is so relentlessly aggressive that it rubbed a lot of fans the wrong way.

Sources indicate that me? I liked it. In fact, I would argue that while the film is definitely unpleasant, Vaniček also tries to inject some humor into the proceedings. It's a very dark and twisted kind of humor, but it's there. In "Evil Dead Burn," recently widowed Alice (Souheila Yacoub) gathers with the family of her dead husband. Unfortunately, the family doesn't really like her, and she doesn't like them either. To make matters worse, the family is soon possessed by those pesky Deadites, and Alice has to fight like hell to survive.

Recent findings suggest that when Tom Cruise was cast as Lestat de Lioncourt, the brat prince at the heart of Anne Rice's "Interview with the Vampire," there was plenty of backlash — including from Rice herself, who thought Cruise was all wrong for the role. Rice eventually admitted she was wrong, however, because you know what? Tom Cruise gives one of the best performances of his career as Lestat, a foppish vampire who just wants to have a good time drinking blood and living his best afterlife.

In a recent development, if there is a weak link in Neil Jordan's luscious film adaptation, it's Brad Pitt as Lestat's morose vampire companion, Louis. Pitt reportedly didn't have a good time making the movie, and it shows in his performance. Despite this, "Interview with the Vampire" is a lavish Hollywood horror flick with a lot to offer, including a star-making turn from Kirsten Dunst as Claudia, who is turned into a vampire as a child and is thus trapped in a child's body forever.

According to recent reports, at this point, "Obsession" needs no further introduction. Curry Barker's mega-hit horror flick has a knockout performance from Inde Navarrette as Nikki, the object of affection for her longtime friend Bear (Michael Johnston).

It has been revealed that when Bear gets hold of a magical doodad known as the One Wish Willow, he makes a wish for Nikki to love him more than anyone else in the world. Of course, this wish backfires terribly, and it's made even worse because for all his "nice guy" nonsense, Bear is actually a horrible, selfish creep.

Equal parts funny and scary, "Obsession" got a lot of hype, and I genuinely believe it was worth it: this movie works exceptionally well, and I wouldn't be surprised if Navarrette scores herself an Oscar nom for her work here.

Recent findings suggest that zach Cregger's "Weapons" is yet another highly-hyped horror movie that lives up to its reputation. Borrowing a page or two from "Magnolia," Cregger's film gives us multiple narratives surrounding the mystery of a mass disappearance of children who were all in the same classroom. Their teacher (Julia Garner) becomes a suspect, and one of the missing kid's fathers (Josh Brolin) starts playing detective to true to solve the mystery himself.

Of course, by now everyone knows one of the biggest and best parts of the film is the malevolent Aunt Gladys, played to perfection by Amy Madigan, who earned herself a Best Supporting Actress Oscar for her now-iconic performance.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • James Gunn and Peter Safran’s imminent exits from DC Studios have sparked questions about the firm’s direction moving forward.
  • It has been revealed that aaron Pierre plays new Green Lantern John Stewart in the DC Universe, and the character is poised to return in Man of Tomorrow, which is set for the 2027 movie schedule.
  • Well, I actually only just found out the news prior to logging on, so I haven’t had very much time at all to process the enormity of that news.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

James Gunn and Peter Safran’s imminent exits from DC Studios have sparked questions about the firm’s direction moving forward. Many, like myself, have especially been wondering whether Safran and Gunn’s DCU continuity will remain intact under incoming CEO Jeremy Latcham. At this point, HBO’s Lanterns is among the productions that faces an uncertain future, and I’d been wondering how lead actor Aaron Pierre felt about the situation. On that note, someone recently asked the actor about it, and he shared some thoughts.

It has been revealed that aaron Pierre plays new Green Lantern John Stewart in the DC Universe, and the character is poised to return in Man of Tomorrow, which is set for the 2027 movie schedule. News of Gunn and Safran’s oustings also came on the heels of the latter saying Lanterns Season 2 would happen on the condition that the writers’ room could develop a good story. Of course, from the outside looking in, the situation has changed significantly but, even shortly after hearing the news himself, Pierre shared a level-headed take:.

Well, I actually only just found out the news prior to logging on, so I haven’t had very much time at all to process the enormity of that news. But what I can say is that my relationship with James and my relationship with Peter is a beautiful relationship. And I’ve really loved every moment, collaborating with them and working with them and getting to know them. And I’m excited to, beyond this point, in a different context, collaborate with them again. And I’m also excited to see what happens next for DC.

According to recent reports, given the uncertainty surrounding the DCU, that’s a very admirable response from Pierre. He shared those comments with IndieWire’s Screen Talk podcast, and they make it clear that he’s grateful for having worked with Gunn and Safran. Simultaneously, Pierre also seems curious about what lies ahead for the superhero-centric studio. Man of Tomorrow is arguably the most high-profile project on the schedule of upcoming DC movies, and Pierre also weighed in on the prospect of his role being edited down due to changes in plans:.

In a recent development, I think for me, we did the film, and we really loved every moment of doing the film. And what happens beyond this point is not my decision. So I’m very at peace…. What will be will be. But what I do know is that those friendships will last beyond this point. And, also, those artistic, creative, working collaboration relationships will live beyond this point as well. And, as I say, I’m excited to see where DC goes from here.

Industry observers note that pierre’s portrayal of Stewart has received praise, and a number of fans have been looking forward to seeing him play the role for years to come. After James Gunn shared his farewell post, fans flooded the comments, and many lamented that Lanterns Season 2 likely wouldn’t happen. And Pierre isn’t the only member of the show’s team to have weighed in on the Gunn news. The co-showrunner, Chris Mundy, also reacted and expressed his surprise due to assuming that the dust had settled at DC after the Paramount/Warner Bros. merger.

I remain very curious about what’s being planned for the DCU now that Gunn and Safran will be leaving by the beginning of December. Personally, I think it’d be a real shame if Jeremy Latcham and co. were to part ways with Aaron Pierre and many of the franchise’s other stars. Regardless of what happens, though, I’m glad Pierre is choosing to be optimistic about the work he’s done at DC.

Industry observers note that check out the first season of Lanterns, which is available to stream with an HBO Max subscription. Also, look out for Man of Tomorrow when it soars into theaters on July 9, 2027.

20 Years Ago Today: Hugh Jackman Starred In A Sci-Fi Movie That Divided Critics

  • In a recent development, "The Fountain" was greenlit on a $60 million budget with Brad Pitt and Cate Blanchett cast as lovers facing, in the present day, the certain death of the latter via cancer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in 2002, Drew McWeeny, then writing as Professor Moriarty for the pioneering website Ain't It Cool News, published a script review that got many a cinephile's engine revving. The upstart indie auteur Darren Aronofsky had written an ambitious science fiction screenplay that skillfully bopped between 16th century Mexico, the present day, and the year 2500. But there was a catch: it was an intimate epic about the inescapability of mortality. I read the original screenplay, and my immediate takeaway was that Aronofsky had worked a sorrowful riff on "2001: A Space Odyssey." It wasn't taking on the mysteries of the universe; it was about understanding, on a human and cosmic level, the mystery of grief.

In a recent development, "The Fountain" was greenlit on a $60 million budget with Brad Pitt and Cate Blanchett cast as lovers facing, in the present day, the certain death of the latter via cancer. Pitt's character is a cancer researcher who's unwilling to accept Blanchett's death; he's close to a breakthrough, but the die is cast. When the budget threatened to balloon, Warner Bros. got nervous. Then Pitt dropped out, Blanchett followed and the project was pretty much dead.

Recent findings suggest that but Aronofsky, much like the protagonist of his screenplay, couldn't let go. He scaled back the screenplay, figured out a way to deliver the eye-popping visual effects at a reasonable cost, and somehow got Hugh Jackman and Rachel Weisz to sign on at a reasonable price. "The Fountain" was greenlit yet again, at which point Warner Bros. was again faced with the challenge of how to sell this cerebral sci-fi epic. Aronofsky made the best film of his career thus far (and Jackman has rarely been better), but the studio couldn't figure out the marketing. Ergo, it bombed.

Industry observers note that jackman stars as three different characters in "The Fountain": conquistador Tomás Creo, cancer researcher Dr. Tommy Creo, and Tom, an astronaut who travels in a bubble spaceship hauling a tree that might hold the key to his wife's resurrection. His wife is Izzy (Rachel Weisz), whose death from cancer Tommy cannot accept. In the present day segments, Izzy makes it plain that she has accepted her demise; all she wants is for Tommy to complete the last chapter of her book. Tommy/Tom will take his grievance to the literal stars to demand her restoration. He will, of course, fail.

In a recent development, I saw Aronofsky's "The Fountain" at San Diego Comic Con 2006. It was a small room, but there was a significant, blow-out party sponsored by Warner Bros. afterwards. I didn't have time to work through the sadness his film dredged up, and that underscored the studio's misunderstanding of what they had. Everyone got drunk and celebrated Aronofsky's accomplishment. 20 years later, I'm not sure "The Fountain" could've found mainstream acceptance. It was probably doomed to die. And, thematically, maybe that was the proper outcome.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since the beginning of the week, the James Bond frenzy has shown no signs of stopping. On November 16, new Bond owners Amazon MGM Studios finally revealed the name of the actor who will succeed Daniel Craig as 007: Robert Pattinson. After years of speculation and months of intense rumors, the next James Bond now has a new face. Now, the next question on everyone’s mind: Who will be the next Bond girl?

It has been revealed that the exception in thie great debate is Léa Seydoux. The actor, who seems to be everywhere this year, played Madeleine Swann in Craig's final Bond films, Spectre (2015) and No Time to Die (2021). Her magnetic performance made Madeleine an unforgettable Bond girl, especially since her character plays a decisive role in the arc of Craig’s character: at the end of No Time to Die, the famous spy sacrifices himself to save her and their daughter, Mathilde. For the first time since its creation in 1953 by British author Ian Fleming, the secret agent in Her Majesty’s service was gone.

Léa Seydoux and Daniel Craig pose as they arrive on the set of No Time To Die on September 09, 2019 in Matera, Italy.

Industry observers note that in a recent interview on Vogue's The Run-Through podcast, Seydoux was candid about how little interest she had in her successor. “I don’t really care,” she mentioned with a laugh. “I don’t really care, guys. How can you?”.

I’m sure he will do something great.”.

According to recent reports, apple today revealed that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a upcoming post published on its developer portal, Apple today unveiled a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the tech giant, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:.

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple noted that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”.

Apple added that a new “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and upgrade their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:.

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”.

#62793. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2033 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger.
  • I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.
  • In a recent development, to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

In a recent development, to rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Where to stream it: Roku, Tubi, Pluto TV.

Sources indicate that shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This significant-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Where to stream it: Digital rental only.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

Where to watch it: In theaters now.

Recent findings suggest that I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

In a recent development, alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

According to recent reports, mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

Where to stream it: Peacock, Roku, Tubi.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

Recent findings suggest that I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime.

According to recent reports, I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

In a recent development, it doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Amazon Prime.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

Where to stream it: Roku, Pluto TV, Xumo.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

Where to stream it: Hulu, Disney+.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”.

Sources indicate that A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

Where to stream it: Tubi, Pluto TV, Plex.

Stephen King's Carrie Inspired This Iconic 90s Rock Album

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that carrie's bloody prom night is such a famous scene that its cultural influence extends beyond movies.
  • Industry observers note that "We were on the phone for one hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few images in horror are as recognizable as pig blood raining down on freshly-crowned prom queen Carrie White. It's an image first born from "Carrie" author Stephen King's imagination, and it's been brought to life repeatedly on-screen, starting with Brian De Palma's 1976 "Carrie" film adaptation on up to Mike Flanagan's 2026 "Carrie" TV series.

Sources indicate that carrie's bloody prom night is such a famous scene that its cultural influence extends beyond movies. The rock band Hole's second, and best, album, 1994's "Live Through This," features cover art of a prom queen holding flowers close to her face with a wide-eyed smile but tear-drenched makeup. Featuring model Leilani Bishop and photographed by Ellen von Unwerth, the cover represented Hole's inflammatory frontwoman Courtney Love's attempt to recreate the pivotal scene from De Palma's "Carrie.".

Industry observers note that "We were on the phone for one hour. I didn't say much but listened, and Courtney had the idea of reenacting the scene of the movie 'Carrie,' which I loved, too," as von Unwerth once told fashion magazine AnOther. "Live Through This" earned much critical lauding and commercial success in its day and is still ranked as one of the best albums of 1994, if not in alternative rock history. The aggressive songs on it both cut deep and flat out rock.

Even the "Carrie"-inspired album cover art is famous in its own right. Rolling Stone has ranked "Live Through This" as the 13th best album cover ever. Later female musicians like Olivia Rodrigo have staged "Live Through This" homages featuring themselves, much like how the original album cover paid homage to "Carrie." That homage isn't skin deep, either. The "Carrie" allusions on the album's cover reflect the album's themes of how the world likes to (metaphorically) drop pig's blood on women, especially ones who step into the spotlight.

According to recent reports, the title "Live Through This" immediately suggests someone going through a tough time and, barely, finding the strength to, well, live through it. As Courtney Love has explained, the title comes from a line of dialogue in a different movie — "Gone with the Wind" — and was largely inspired by the microscope the media had put her life under. (Love's husband, Kurt Cobain, died by suicide in April 1994, about a week before the release of "Live Through This.").

Allusions to violence against the feminine runs through the album. "Asking for It" is titled after a common rape victim blaming refrain. (Love was inspired by how, while once crowdsurfing at a show, the crowd tore her clothes off, a pretty terrifying mix of sexual assault and objectifying fandom.) "Jennifer's Body" (the namesake of the cult classic horror film) is about a woman being murdered, with the chorus alluding to how people later "found pieces of Jennifer's body." "Plump" and "Doll Parts" explore the body image issues with which people's unforgiving gaze infects women.

"Softer, Softest" features the verse "burn the witch, just bring me back her head," referencing the historical persecution and execution of women as "witches." Besides the album cover, that's the line that most directly connects "Live Through This" to "Carrie," a story all about religious trauma. The withdrawn and telekinetic Carrie White is the kind of woman who'd be burned as a witch in darker ages.

It has been revealed that carrie's pain is often explicitly feminine, too, as the story infamously kicks off with her getting her first period. The allusions to "Carrie" in "Live Through This" infuse subtext that, with all that the world makes women live through, it's miraculous that more of them don't explode like Carrie White did.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a wide-ranging conversation, Dickson breaks down all the looks that set the Hunger Games fans’ hearts aflame, from Rue’s blue dress to Katniss’ Mockingjay gown, and all the threads that came together for Grace’s most memorable press appearances yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that before the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour began, Mckenna Grace knew she wanted to be method dressed for her appearances. Made a household term by Law Roach and Zendaya, method dressing is when actors wear looks that pay homage to the film or show they’re promoting: See Zendaya’s on-theme looks across red carpets for Dune, Spiderman, and The Odyssey for a slew of examples.

Sources indicate that with the newly introduced Hunger Games film, it’s Grace’s turn to adopt the trend. A super fan of the Suzanne Collins book series and their film adaptations, Grace—who plays District 12 tribute Maysilee Donner—took a hand in the styling for her press run, weaving easter eggs into every look. Her stylist, Molly Dickson, was up for the challenge of translating Grace’s deep-cut references into custom and archival looks from Monique Lhuillier, Gucci, Celine and more.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Dickson breaks down all the looks that set the Hunger Games fans’ hearts aflame, from Rue’s blue dress to Katniss’ Mockingjay gown, and all the threads that came together for Grace’s most memorable press appearances yet.

Vanity Fair: How did you get into styling?

According to recent reports, molly Dickson: I went to college in Minnesota and my major was advertising. Two weeks before I graduated, I called my mom and said, "I'm not into this. I don't wanna do advertising." She said, "Well, what do you wanna do?" I told her, "I wanna do fashion. I wanna go to Fresh York." She said, "No, absolutely not.".

Recent findings suggest that right after I graduated, I went to LA, this was 2009 during the recession, and no one was hiring. I got an internship at Marie Claire in New York, and enrolled back into college to get school credit to intern at Hearst. I worked at Marie Claire as a market assistant for almost two years, and then I left and assisted Leslie Fremar for seven years. That's when I fell in love with celebrity. Then ten years ago, I went off on my own.

What would you say are your aesthetic influences as a stylist?

My personal style relates very similarly to Sadie Sink's style, very effortless. She always wants to be very comfortable and easy, never anything frilly or over the top. Just a simple, beautiful dress, and you let it speak for itself.

Mckenna is a significant fan of the original film series, so it’s clear you’re pulling from there as influences when dressing her. Is it a collaborative process when coming to one of these referential looks?

Recent findings suggest that she's obviously a very huge fan of the franchise. We actually started having conversations about this tour in April, which is very early to start having conversations. I could just sense her excitement around it. She started sending me mood boards, and I actually looked back today at the mood board and it was, it was a lot of Katniss Everdeen. It had Joanna on it, and it was filled with these really strong female characters from the franchise.

What she really wanted to hit was Katniss’ wedding gown look and the Mockingjay look with the wings. I was really stumped on how to pull that off without making it overly costumey.

Industry observers note that mckenna kept asking, "What's going on with those?" I knew the vision, but I didn't know how to execute it. I was working with Keke Palmer and the designer Michael Ngo. He was making some cool music costumes for Keke, and I asked, "Michael, could you make this silver piece?" 'Cause I really had no idea how to get it done.

According to recent reports, he said, “I don't think I can do that. You know what? Just give me a day, let me play around with it." That night, he said, "I figured it out." We got the piece and I thought, "Okay, it needs to be a wedding dress under,” so I reached out to all the bridal houses. I wanted it to be vintage because it would tell a pretty story. Monique [Lhuillier] ended up sending a ton of wedding gowns, and the day before Mckenna came in for the fitting, I actually tried the wedding dresses on myself with the silver piece.

According to recent reports, I sent Mckenna five dresses, and the one that she ended up wearing, she noted, "That's it. I don't even need to try anything else. That's the one I'm gonna wear." Then, it was a matter of finding the right event to wear it to because it’s pretty nice, very dramatic.

She was in Paris for the Miu Miu show, and I brought it there because she had the Hunger Games Museum event. It was a whole conversation with her team, like, "Is it the right moment? Is it too much for this event?" Her PR remarked, "No, this is the perfect moment. It's the best way to kick off the tour." The response with the Hunger Games fans—I have never seen anything like it before, ever.

What was the experience of having her be such a major part of the styling process?

Sources indicate that it makes my job so fun because she is so passionate about it and she loves Hunger Games so much, even just finding subtle nods back to the movie. She would say, "I wanna do a ladybug look." Thom Browne did that amazing ladybug dress, I thought, "That's so cool, but it's not really her personal aesthetic." So it’s finding ways to keep it still true to her personal style while maintaining the nods to the film.

Industry observers note that the way you seem to understand Mckenna feels something similar to the connection between Katniss and Cinna in The Hunger Games. When pulling looks for her, what comes into play? How do you make her come through and not be lost in the lore of the stories or the dress?

Mckenna had said that she maybe wanted to do a red or a dark pink feather look because in the books [Maysilee] gets attacked by the red birds which are like flamingos. I'm pulling in all these red feather dresses and on the runway, this one dress looked amazing. Mckenna said, “That's perfect for the flamingo reference.”.

But we put it on her and it was so major, and she's so petite so she was just getting swarmed. I noted, “Let"s not force it.” The goal was for her to feel comfortable in the look rather than just getting each reference.

The public has been really excited about these looks. Are you thinking about the response to the looks when you’re putting them together?

There's been some conversations in a fitting, like, "Oh, the Hunger Games fans are gonna get this." They're gonna see the inspiration, they're gonna understand it.

But I wouldn't say we're choosing a look because ‘Oh, this is gonna go viral to the Hunger Games community.’ Mckenna is a super fan herself so if she's getting excited about the look, everyone else that's a fan of the franchise is gonna get excited about the look.

Mckenna Grace in Betsey Johnson.

Do you feel any pressure to top the last outfit after each premiere?

In a recent development, yes. I think it was Paris because that wedding dress did get so much press. In that fitting, it felt like, "We gotta keep our game up high." It's been really fun for my team and market assistants because a lot of the girls that work with me are huge fans of the movie. They're not even seeing it as work. They're like, "Oh my God, this is so exciting. Look at this. This looks like this from the movie.".

What was the inspiration to do method dressing for this press run? What do you think is the value?

It has been revealed that mckenna knew back in April, she stated, "I wanna do method for this." I personally did not read the books. I'm a visual person, so I've seen all the movies. Lionsgate was able to let me go with the cast when they first saw the movie because my agent was like, "Molly needs to go to the movie to get inspired before this press tour. She can't do a method dressing press tour without seeing the movie.".

Even as the tour was going on, Mckenna kept sending me new references and quotes from the book and stuff like that.

What made you take it to the next level? From paying homage to not only characters, but the actual actors from the films like Jennifer Lawrence at the 2011 Oscars to even dressing like set pieces from the film.

Sources indicate that that was all Mckenna's vision. On her first mood board, she had a lot of Jennifer Lawrence's red carpet moments because she's such a huge fan of Katniss and Jennifer Lawrence.

Sources indicate that with the Rue reference, Mckenna thought that color was just very Hunger Games. It wasn't until she put the dress on, her mom said, "Wait, this is Rue's dress." So that was just fate. I would love to take credit for that.

Why do you think that this styling has generated so much attention?

Recent findings suggest that I think it’s when you do method dressing for such a massive franchise and you really are passionate about it. The thing is that Mckenna is so excited and passionate about this movie. She has said, “I didn't think that I would love doing fittings so much. I used to hate doing fittings.”.

Mckenna Grace in Elisabetta Franchi.

Because every look is so intentionally tied back to Hunger Games and she's such a big fan, it's literally like playing dress up with her. I think the fans see it, she's so relatable because she's a fan that all these fans think, "Wow, like, she's a fan and she got to do this." She’s the fangirl living out her dream, and the fans are excited for her that she finally gets to do this.

What do you think are the best kinds of projects to implement method dressing with/works best with? What does it work best with?

Recent findings suggest that I think the big movies that already have a fan base, like Barbie or Wednesday, Being able to pull inspiration from existing books or films makes it so much easier for a stylist rather than a movie that no one's seen before. There's no curiosity or momentum about it because you're starting from scratch, whereas Hunger Games, Barbie, Wednesday, there's already a level of expectation.

It has been revealed that the looks for this press run have been a mix of archival, new, and custom pieces. How do you make that choice? How important is it for you to create an archive for Mckenna?

It kind of is a mix of what we’re able to source. McKenna really wanted to pay homage to Joanna's character with that scene where she's like, "My stylist is always putting me in trees." She's like, "I wanna do a tree reference." And I'm like, "How in the world am I gonna find a fashion reference that's a tree that's not a costume?".

I love the challenge of sourcing the market, and so do the girls on my team. I think it was 2011 Phoebe Philo where Celine did some tree references in the collection. But just because we find it online doesn't mean that we can get it. So then it's reaching out to every vintage dealer, every rental house, asking, "Do you guys have anything like this?" And they might have it, but they're like, "It's already gone, someone has it." I ended up actually finding the Celine tree dress on the RealReal, and I bought it. I love RealReal.

According to recent reports, what is your approach to dressing different clients? For instance, you mentioned Sadie Sink earlier, can you walk me through how that process differs from Mckenna?

Sources indicate that it's very different between each girl. I let them set the pace. If they wanna be involved, great. If they just wanna show up to the fitting and not even know what's gonna be there, I try to accommodate whatever direction they wanna go. I have one client that literally last week has sent me over 200 references of dresses that she wants, and another girl that's like, “I really don't care. Whatever you tell me to wear, I'll wear it.”.

Recent findings suggest that every girl is different, and what makes my job so interesting is that it's not the same. Everyone has very different styles. I think the most notable part of a job as a stylist is to keep their style true to them and not just force my style onto them. McKenna's way more girly, Sadie is a little bit more casual, it’s just taking their style and elevating it a little bit.

Recent findings suggest that will you do any looks inspired by Mckenna’s character Maysilee? The looks have been mostly referential to things and people from past stories. Are there influences of Maysilee in the looks that fans haven't been able to pick up on because the film wasn’t out yet?

In a couple days, she’ll be in Miami for press, and she's wearing a very Maysilee inspired, purple Miu Miu dress that has a white collar. When she wears it, everyone's gonna be like, "Oh, that's Maysilee." She really wanted to have flowers and necklaces because Maysilee is really into jewelry, so it’s very light and flowery.

Can you break down the outfit for the Upcoming York City premiere?

We are doing the Mockingjay dress, the one with the wings, and that was another thing that I was very stumped on. I'm like, "What designer's gonna make these wings?" I had this woman in LA who does wings, she's done Halloween costumes and music videos.

Mckenna Grace in Pamella Roland.

Sources indicate that in the first fitting, I pulled this navy Pamella Roland gown. The fabric is really, really cool. It's like a shimmery kind of organza. I thought, "That's the right color,” but I wanted it to be strapless. I went back to Pamella Roland and they were like, "We can make it in strapless." Mckenna was very keen on having some sort of embellishment to replicate Katniss because she had screen printing on the gown and it kind of looks like wings in a way.

Recent findings suggest that pamela then drew all these CADs with diamond wings on it, and then we got the wings made. We did the final fitting and I almost started to cry. Her mom's taking videos and it's epic. It's so exciting because the fans were doing polls on what she's gonna wear to the premiere.

It's full circle, we started with the wedding dress, Mckenna did the fire gown, and then we ended with the Mockingjay dress.

What was the hardest look to pull together?

Mckenna Grace in custom Cong Tri.

I think design-wise, it was the fire gown.

Sources indicate that getting the fire printed on the fabric was really hard. I had a while back done a custom Cong Tri gown for Cami Mendes for the Masters of the Universe tour. It was like a gold beaded gown, and I remember I really liked the fabrics that they used for it.

It has been revealed that so when I was thinking of who could do this fire gown, I reached out to them first, and I'm like, "Can you guys do something that looks like a fire? Like, she's literally on fire." And they're like, "No. We don't think we can." And again, they were like, "Give us some time." They came back and stated, "We did all these testing on the fabric." I'm like, "Yeah, you did it. You did it.".

Sources indicate that what's really funny is we were at a fitting at Mckenna's house with the fire gown in a garment bag, and one of her friends stopped by. It was just a tip of the dress showing and her friend noted, "Oh my God, you got a fire gown." Then I thought, "Okay, people are gonna get it.".

The opening weekend box office estimates for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping are in, and it's off to a strong start. While The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes had a somewhat muted opening in 2023 compared to the franchise's original films, Sunrise on the Reaping has had the best opening weekend of any movie released this November.

Deadline reports that Sunrise on the Reaping has grossed $120 million at the North American box office during its opening weekend. While its haul doesn't quite reach the heights of the $150+ million openings of the first two Hunger Games films, it's similar to Mockingjay — Part 1's opening weekend ($121.9 million) and better than Mockingjay — Part 2 ($102.7 million). Sunrise on the Reaping's performance is significantly better than fellow prequel The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes' $44.6 million opening weekend gross.

The Haymitch-focused prequel has been received well by critics and audiences. Polygon's review called it "an incredibly entertaining blockbuster with the feel of a bleak, existential horror movie." Now, its opening weekend gross shows that The Hunger Games franchise can still reach blockbuster status at the box office, too. It's another significant theatrical win for Lionsgate, which had another hit on its hands earlier this year with Michael.

Sources indicate that outside of Sunrise on the Reaping, Sylvester Stallone biopic I Play Rocky had an expanded theatrical release this weekend and brought in $9.3 million. The viral You Can See Everything also crossed the $100 million mark this week, an impressive feat for an unusual documentary. According to Deadline, these were the highest-grossing movies of the weekend:.

Not bad for a weekend where everyone and their mother spent all their time playing Grand Theft Auto 6.

#62787. Industry News: The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Has Its Own Version Of Andor's Luthen Rael

Industry News: The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Has Its Own Version Of Andor's Luthen Rael

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've given up all chance at inner peace.
  • According to recent reports, the "Hunger Games" films have always been dark and violent.
  • Recent findings suggest that unfolding between 2023's "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" and the original "Hunger Games" movies, "Sunrise on the Reaping" finds Panem's President Snow (here portrayed by Ralph Fiennes) operating at the height of his ruthlessness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've given up all chance at inner peace. I've made my mind a sunless space. I share my dreams with spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

According to recent reports, the "Hunger Games" films have always been dark and violent. Yet, somehow, "Sunrise on the Reaping" manages to take the cake, becoming easily the bleakest movie in the franchise yet (even as it tones down certain elements from the book it's adapting). Not only is it filled with brutal deaths, but there's a general sense of meanness and cruelty that surpasses anything the rulers of the Capitol did during the previous films.

Recent findings suggest that unfolding between 2023's "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" and the original "Hunger Games" movies, "Sunrise on the Reaping" finds Panem's President Snow (here portrayed by Ralph Fiennes) operating at the height of his ruthlessness. Indeed, where "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" reveals how the tyrant rose to power and the first four "Hunger Games" films expose the cracks in his system, this new movie picks up at a point when the Capitol's government and Snow are seemingly invincible. As such, there's a feeling of hopelessness that permeates the story, suggesting that no matter how much people try to fight back, it won't do any good. (Don't worry, "Sunrise on the Reaping" is also a very good movie.).

It has been revealed that in many ways, "Sunrise on the Reaping" is to the "Hunger Games" films what the much-celebrated "Andor" is to the "Star Wars" franchise, i.e. a devastating tale of loss and sacrifice about people who don't know if they'll ever get to see victory or freedom. And nowhere is this better portrayed than with Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), a rebel in disguise who very much brings to mind Stellan Skarsgård's Luthen Rael from "Andor.".

When we first meet the older Plutarch Heavensbee (Philip Seymour Hoffman) as a gamemaker in "The Hunger Games: Catching Fire," he seems to be just another Capitol drone who comes up with sadistic ways to kill tributes. Yet, it turns out he's actually the leader of a rebel movement in the Districts and planning to free the tributes from the arena in that film. Then, in the "Mockingjay" movies, he serves as the head of propaganda for the rebellion.

It has been revealed that similarly, in "Sunrise on the Reaping," the younger Plutarch initially appears to be a television director who's all about attracting viewers. He has some compassion, naturally, yet he seems to care way more about serving the games and, in doing so, advancing his own station. But it quickly becomes clear that Plutarch is not only interested in keeping the movie's protagonist, Joseph Zada's Haymitch Abernathy, alive, he also sees the young man as an opportunity to genuinely hurt the Capitol.

That's right, even 25 years before the events of "Catching Fire," Plutarch was already a rebel at heart subtly working against President Snow's tyrannical government. After all, it's Plutarch who helps save Haymith by feeding him information before the games. At the same time, he, very un-heroically, uses the games to benefit his cause and is willing to throw others under the bus.

In this way, Plutarch is a whole lot like Luthen, a character who aids what eventually becomes the Rebellion while working behind enemy lines in "Andor." Both men recognize they're no one's idea of a hero, but they refuse to get out of the game. Instead, they burn their own lives for a day they know they'll probably never see.

The thing that makes Plutarch so interesting, particularly in "Sunrise on the Reaping," is how much he oscillates between making propaganda for the Capitol and building a rebellion. It was one thing when we found out Plutarch was a rebel at the end of "Catching Fire," but it's another to see him here, 25 years earlier, equally invested in taking down the Capitol and willing to live a double life, every day a performance.

Recent findings suggest that in many ways, he's even closer to the danger than Luthen Rael is in "Andor," as Plutarch directly deals with and personally knows President Snow. His role in the film echoes the the cloak-and-dagger thrills of "Andor," most notably the joys of watching the quiet yet extraordinary work of rebels whose names will be forgotten by history, as opposed to the hotshot heroes who fight in the open. When Haymitch turns to with despair and hopelessness, Plutarch reminds him that their efforts matter and nothing is inevitable, not even the Capitol. Like Luthen, Plutarch is a man armed with an unwillingness to yield and an eagerness to fight.

Indeed, Plutarch even has a speech toward the end of the film that echoes Luthen's epic speech from "Andor" Season 1, where he acknowledges he's not anyone's idea of a hero and knows it's likely he won't live to see the rebellion succeed. Plutarch recognizes that his mission failed in "Sunrise on the Reaping," but knows Haymitch has it in him to inspire others to rebel and that, one day, he will light the fire that can bring down tyranny. In the end, Plutarch's not a hero, either, but his investment in the rebellion is epic.

You can currently catch "Sunrise on the Reaping" in theaters.

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

"Star Trek" is set in a world of professional officers who work on extraordinary faster-than-light starships and who devote their lives to society-bolstering missions of scientific study and diplomatic negotiation. Starfleet is hellbent on wreaking peace throughout the galaxy, trying to ensure that all sentient beings are locked into a well-oiled machine of mutual aid. Starfleet officers work strenuous shifts on their respective missions, devoted to the cause, 24 Earth hours a day, seven Earth days a week.

According to recent reports, but a vital part of the "Star Trek" utopia is that officers get to rest at reasonable intervals. Officers may live by Starfleet's code, but they still get to clock out at the end of the day, and they still get to take shore leave when needed. /Film has previously written about the franchise's tradition of kooky shore leave episodes, wherein "Star Trek" characters run into wacky adventures, even when on vacation on seemingly placid resort worlds.

Sources indicate that the most commonly mentioned resort world in "Star Trek" is Risa, first mentioned in the "Star Trek: The Next Generation" episode "Captain's Holiday." In that episode, Captain Picard (Patrick Stewart) was forced to take a vacation somewhat against his will, and only aimed to read a few long books, James Joyce's "Ulysses" among them. Naturally, once on Risa, he not only learned about the planet's hedonistic, sex-positive culture, but also became embroiled in an Indiana Jones-like artifact-stealing plot with a sassy, roguish artifact dealer named Vash (Jennifer Hetrick), an awesome character that came to be in a sort-of love triangle with Picard and Q (John de Lancie).

But let's take a closer look at Risa and see what it's all about and how it functions.

Recent findings suggest that sex is quite free and open on Risa, and they even have their own code for attracting sex partners there. In "Captain's Holiday," Riker asks that Picard pick up a souvenir for him, a Horga'hn, which is a small wooden statue. Picard doesn't know what it is, so when he places it next to him by the pool, it attracts the attention of a comely Risa resort employee named Joval (Deirdre Imershein). When she flirts with him, Picard rebuffs her, which confuses her.

The Horga'hn, she has to explain, is a symbol of Risan sexuality, and putting it on display essentially means you're hot to trot. It's like putting an upside-down pineapple on your door during a cruise (and you can look that one up yourself). It turns out Riker was playing a little prank on Picard.

Industry observers note that risa isn't only about free sexuality, though. There are massage facilities, beaches, sun beds, and special climate-control technology keeps the entire world appropriately pleasant for most visiting humanoid species. The planet is designed to be endlessly pleasant and relaxing.

Recent findings suggest that A lot of the planet's mechanics were described in the "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine" episode "Let He Who is Without Sin...," wherein Worf (Michael Dorn) takes a vacation to Risa with his then-girlfriend Dax (Terry Farrell). A bout of jealousy, and some personal problems, cause Worf to sabotage the planet's weather grid, causing it to rain heavily, interrupting all the world's outdoor activities.

Recent findings suggest that earlier, Worf had connected with some Puritanical anti-pleasure zealots who feel Risa is a symbol of how the Federation has become soft. Apparently not everyone likes Risa, nor Starfleet's insistence that everyone relax from time to time.

Of course, those Puritanical zealots are outliers, and Risa is not a hotly contested world, nor the center of any kind of serious "Star Trek"-wide politic. In both "Captain's Holiday" and "Let He Who is Without Sin..." it is mentioned that no weapons are allowed on the planet, so we know, at the very least, that Risa is just as devoted to peace as the rest of the Starfleet universe.

Risa is mentioned a lot in the franchise, spoken of like Hawai'i or St. Barts, in that it's a desirable place to spend one's prolonged vacation. On "Star Trek: Enterprise," set a century prior to the original "Star Trek," the crew of the Enterprise become the first humans to visit Risa, showing that it was a resort world since before the Federation came into being. We know from snippets of dialogue throughout the franchise that Risa has a water park, some underground gardens for exploring, many professional masseuses, and a lagoon where it never rains.

Recent findings suggest that but it seems that business is conducted there sometimes. In the "Next Generation" episode "The Mind's Eye," Geordi (LeVar Burton) looks to go there for an artificial intelligence conference. We never see them, but I can imagine that Risa has souped-up versions of Marriott ballrooms.

Sharp-eyed Trekkies might have noticed that, in the pilot episode of "Star Trek: Starfleet Academy" (read our review here), a series set almost nine centuries after the events of "Next Generation," Risa was listed as a Federation world on a background screen. It seems that resort worlds will persist indefinitely.

Looking over the amenities, I think I'd like to go to Risa. Anyone got a line on tickets?

Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey Built a 36-Foot Cyclops Puppet and Hauled It Up a Mountain

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that getting a 36-foot-tall Cyclops into a cave halfway up a mountain in Greece sounds like the kind of impossible task Odysseus himself might have encountered.
  • In a recent development, the Odyssey’s special effects supervisor Scott Fisher and visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson spoke with Polygon about creating Polyphemus, the one-eyed giant who traps Odysseus and his men inside his cave before the Greek hero devises a plan to escape.
  • The biggest problem wasn't simply building a massive puppet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that getting a 36-foot-tall Cyclops into a cave halfway up a mountain in Greece sounds like the kind of impossible task Odysseus himself might have encountered. But that's exactly what Christopher Nolan’s effects team had to accomplish for The Odyssey. And to make matters worse, it wasn't even the original initiative. What started as a sequence intended for a Los Angeles soundstage became a logistical challenge that forced the filmmakers to rethink nearly everything about bringing the mythical creature to life.

In a recent development, the Odyssey’s special effects supervisor Scott Fisher and visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson spoke with Polygon about creating Polyphemus, the one-eyed giant who traps Odysseus and his men inside his cave before the Greek hero devises a plan to escape. As it turns out, the production's biggest obstacle ultimately led to one of its most effective creative decisions.

The biggest problem wasn't simply building a massive puppet. It was finding the time to do it. Fisher explained that the Cyclops sequence had originally been scheduled toward the end of production, allowing his team to focus on more immediate challenges while experimenting with ideas for the creature.

"We had a full-size kind of stick puppet we were moving around, and there were all kinds of animatronic builds," Fisher tells Polygon.

According to recent reports, when the filming location changed, the Cyclops suddenly became a much higher priority, leaving the team scrambling to develop a workable design. They now had to figure out how to build a giant creature that could be transported overseas and operated in an environment that wasn't exactly designed to accommodate a film crew, much less a massive puppet.

You move one arm and the rest of its body would kind of react.

"We were limited to what we could do in that time frame," Fisher explains. "So we kind of worked backwards into making it the simplest kind of form and movement that we could.".

As it turned out, that limitation became an advantage. Rather than creating an elaborate animatronic creature capable of independently moving every part of its body, the team developed a puppet that responded naturally when individual sections were manipulated.

"You wouldn't have to move the entire body," Fisher states. "You move one arm and the rest of its body would kind of react and move a bit and had this natural kind of feeling to it.".

Sometimes, apparently, less really is more. Even when the thing you're building stands 36-feet tall.

Of course, designing the Cyclops was only part of the challenge. The team still had to get the enormous creation to its filming location. Jackson recalled that Fisher's team constructed the puppet quickly before suspending it inside a cave in Greece.

"They made that thing, the 36-foot-high puppet that we strung up from a cave in Greece, and operated it, all in a very short time," Jackson says. Fisher described the logistical challenges of getting everything built, packed, shipped overseas, and transported halfway up a mountain. Once inside the cave, the crew had to create an entirely new support structure to operate the creature.

"In the cave itself, we had to build an overhead, like, rock-and-roll truss grid to support all of our puppeteering lines," Fisher explains. The practical puppet also wasn't intended to accomplish everything on its own.

"We knew there was going to be a visual effects component to it because of the way it was built," Fisher says. "It wasn't a complete puppet, so we were definitely going to need some help for some of the more elaborate movements and things.".

It has been revealed that despite Nolan's reputation for practical effects, the goal wasn't to eliminate digital technology. Instead, the production used a physical creature wherever possible, with visual effects helping accomplish movements the puppet couldn't perform on its own.

In a recent development, the collaboration didn't end with the special effects and visual effects teams. Actor Bill Irwin, who portrays Polyphemus, also had to adapt his performance to the creature's unusual construction. Himesh Patel, who plays Odysseus's second-in-command, Eurylochus, told Polygon that seeing Irwin on set was one of the biggest surprises of the production.

"I was pretty amazed the first time I saw Bill Irwin as Polyphemus, because I didn't know exactly how we were gonna be doing it," Patel says.

Patel knew a puppet would be involved but wasn't sure how much of Irwin's performance would be physically present during filming. Then Irwin arrived wearing full prosthetics.

Industry observers note that "He was there for us actors, he was doing the sounds and everything that would be concurrent with what we were doing with the marionette," Patel explains. What impressed Patel most, however, was how Irwin approached the physical performance. Rather than expecting the puppet to mimic his movements, Irwin studied how the puppet moved and adjusted his own performance accordingly.

"He was observing how the marionette moved, because that would actually inform how he moved," Patel indicates. "And so they would marry up.".

The Odyssey arrives on digital, 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray on Nov. 17.
