“Cancer does change you,” Kate Middleton says, emotion clear in her voice. “It changes your body, it changes you physically. But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.” These words come not at as an Instagram post or at a public event. Instead, they're the voice-over in a previously unannounced documentary about the Princess of Wales and her life since she disclosed a diagnosis of cancer in 2024.

According to Kensington Palace, which unveiled the film on Saturday, Heal is “a deeply personal newly introduced documentary from The Princess of Wales, exploring life beyond diagnosis and the many ways people find comfort, strength and hope in the face of serious illness.” It will air on the BBC in the UK on November 29, and in the US on NBCUniversal on November 30.

Heal follows Kate Middleton during her participation in one of the United Kingdom’s most demanding endurance events: The National Three Peaks Challenge, which she completed this summer. In less than 24 hours, the princess climbed the three highest mountains in Scotland, England, and Wales: Ben Nevis (4,413 feet), Scafell Pike (3,209 feet), and Yr Wyddfa–Snowdon (3,559 feet). The undertaking wasn't just a personal effort, as it was also in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization that supports people living with cancer before, during, and after the disease.

The documentary will also support that organization, Kensington Palace notes, saying “All funds received through the documentary's distribution have been directed to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity to help people living with and beyond cancer.” The Royal Marsden Hospital, at which Middleton received treatment, is also referenced in the film, as Middleton's brother, James, asks her “Isn’t it when you leave the Royal Marsden, you ring the bell?”.

Sources indicate that but while many patients participate in the bell-ringing ritual at the conclusion of treatment, Middleton claims she missed out on that moment. “Yeah, but I didn’t ring the bell,” she replies. “So maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” James responded, suggesting her Three Peaks experience was that symbolic peal.

Sources indicate that while Prince William is no stranger to documentary work, nor are Prince Harry and wife Meghan Markle, this is Kate Middleton's first venture into the format. According to recent reports, “Through this documentary, The Princess hopes to help others navigate diagnosis, recovery and life beyond cancer and transform access to holistic cancer care which supports wellbeing, resilience and quality of life during and after diagnosis,” Kensington Palace says of Heal, a message underscored by Middleton's words in the trailer. “You know, healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”.

Sources indicate that anthony Mackie knows how to keep a Marvel press tour interesting, especially when Sebastian Stan's name comes up. The two actors have spent years giving each other grief in interviews, and I have to imagine that, by now, Stan knows better than to expect a compliment when someone hands Mackie a microphone. Still, this bit of friendly trash talk is pretty ruthless. With another Avengers movie closing out the 2026 movie schedule, the former Falcon-turned-Cap has popped up again in a clip ranking his MCU screen partners, and shots have been fired at Stan.

In a recent development, in a resurfaced clip from an episode of Hot Ones Versus that's making the rounds on Instagram, Mackie sits opposite his Captain America: Brave Upcoming World co-star Danny Ramirez. The premise is simple: Answer an uncomfortable question or eat a very spicy wing. Then Ramirez asks Mackie to rank three of his Captain America scene partners from most to least talented. He probably thought he'd finally found a question Mackie wouldn't touch, but as the clip below shows, nothing was stopping Mackie from throwing shade at the Thunderbolts* star. Not even hot wings:.

A post shared by First We Feast (@firstwefeast).

The three names on the list were Chris Evans, Ramirez, and Stan. Essentially, that's a fairly brutal choice for Mackie, considering how long he's worked with Evans and Stan in the MCU, while Ramirez was sitting right there, ready to hear where his new Captain America thought he ranked.

In a recent development, mackie didn't seem all that conflicted, though. Evans, who played Steve Rogers/Cap before Sam Wilson inherited the shield, took the top spot. Ramirez came in second. Then Mackie went after the Winter Soldier actor with an answer that probably needs a little censoring:.

In a recent development, this is so fucked up. [Laughs] From most talented to least talented: Chris Evans, Danny Ramirez, fuck Sebastian Stan. He got a Golden Globe, an Oscar nomination. He got a new girlfriend. He got everything.

According to recent reports, that's one way to rank acting ability. Mackie had good reason to bring up the hardware. Stan won a Golden Globe for his performance in A Different Man in January 2025, and he also earned a Best Actor Oscar nomination for playing Donald Trump in The Apprentice. Both films marked pretty significant moments for an actor many Marvel fans still know primarily as Bucky Barnes. And Mackie was clearly keeping track.

Anyone who's followed these two beyond the release of new Marvel movies knows this is pretty standard behavior. Mackie and Stan first appeared together in 2014's Captain America: The Winter Soldier and, later, their verbal squabbles in 2016's Civil War made a real splash with audiences. Watching Sam and Bucky bicker was also half the fun of their eventual Marvel series, 2021's The Falcon and the Winter Soldier. Their Mackie and Stan's interviews together were sometimes even better.

The funny part is that Mackie has also been one of Stan's biggest cheerleaders. When Stan won that Golden Globe, Mackie famously interrupted his post-win Entertainment Tonight interview to congratulate him. There's video of that, too, and it's hard to square the excitement of that moment with the idea that Mackie actually thinks Stan is the least talented actor in the group.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

As for Ramirez, I can't blame him if he enjoyed the moment. Following his MCU debut as Joaquin Torres in TFATW, his character officially became the new Falcon, opposite Mackie's Captain America in Brave New World. Getting ranked above an Oscar nominee by the guy you're sharing the screen with has to feel pretty good, even if the entire exercise is one major joke.

Personally, I hope Stan finds a reason to return the favor. Both actors are set to return in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday, which hits theaters Dec. 18. As we wait for Cap, his cohorts, and scene partners to return to the big screen, fans can revisit all the Marvel movies with a Disney+ subscription.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, francis Lawrence's latest film "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," the sixth film in the series, takes place 24 years before the events of the first "Hunger Games" and concerns the fate of the teenage Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) as he comes to compete in the 50th Hunger Games. The games are a televised bloodsport featuring teens, put into practice to placate a starving population in a dystopian future. /Film has reviewed "Sunrise on the Reaping," and Nina Starner gave it an eight out of 10.

It has been revealed that one of the side characters in "Sunrise" is a man named Mr. McCoy, the father of one Louella McCoy (Molly McCann) — a friend of Haymitch's whose grim fate leads to one of the most disturbing moments in the whole saga. Mr. McCoy is played by Jefferson White, who "Yellowstone" fans will immediately recognize as series regular Jimmy Hurdstram.

It has been revealed that white played Jimmy in all 53 episodes of "Yellowstone," and his character arc has been fascinating. He was an ex-con who was hired as a ranchhand, and who had to slowly find his footing to outrun his criminal past.

White's first professional screen credit came in 2014 when he appeared in two episodes of "The Americans." He has had a robust TV career ever since, possessed of unique features and a great deal of talent. He climbed through the ranks, making an actor's requisite stop in an episode of "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" and appearing in nine episodes of the Los Alamos-set TV series "Manhattan.".

Recent findings suggest that jefferson White is a hard-working character actor who has managed to stay in the public eye with a promptly growing string of impressive credits over the course of the last decade-plus. He was in an episode of "Elementary," three episodes of "Aquarius," and seven episodes of "How to Get Away with Murder," playing a character named Phillip Jessup. He also appeared on "Blue Bloods," "House of Cards," "The Alienist," and the 2019 reboot of "The Twilight Zone." He had a notable role in the second season of "Blindspot," and appeared in four episodes of the miniseries "The Bite." White seems to have one of those faces that casting directors love, and the talent to back it up.

White's stint on "Yellowstone" lasted from 2018 through 2024, and he has continued to work since. He has appeared on the TV series "Evil," and turned up on demonstrates like "You," "Countdown," "The Hunting Party," and "Boston Blue.".

Recent findings suggest that on film, White's career has been growing as well. In 2022, he appeared in the Thandiwe Newton drama "God's Country," and the following year, he landed a supporting role in William Oldroyd's thriller "Eileen" with Thomasin McKenzie and Anne Hathaway. In 2024, he appeared in Alex Garland's hot-button dystopia film "Civil War" and in the comic book flop "Hellboy: The Crooked Man." In 2025, he played the lead role in a little indie film called "Drink and Be Merry," on which he also served as executive producer.

2026 is a banner year for White, as he not only appears in "Sunrise on the Reaping," but also in Stephanie Ahn's drama "Bedford Park" and in the road movie "The Long Haul" with Margo Martindale, Cole Sprouse, and Stephen Root.

Before he was even cast in the movie, Jefferson White provided the narration for the audiobook of "Sunrise on the Reaping.".

It seems that the "Hunger Games" prequel is just another step in White's career. The actor will also appear as Lee Harvey Oswald in Roland Joffé's JFK drama "November 1963," set for release on December 4. That film also stars John Travolta as real-life gangster Johnny Roselli and Robert Carlyle as Jack Ruby, the nightclub owner who killed Oswald following JFK's assassination.

White is also set to appear in "John Rambo," the "First Blood" prequel starring Noah Centineo as the character originated by Sylvester Stallone. Both I and Stallone agree that "First Blood" is the actor's best action movie, so it will be fascinating to see if "John Rambo" will be any good. That film is currently slated for release on June 4, 2027.

Meanwhile, "Yellowstone" fans can rest easy knowing that White's character, Jimmy Hurdstram, has gone on to have a recurring role on the spinoff series "Marshals." The "Yellowstone" franchise is vast, and spans many years of history, having had spinoffs set in 1883 and 1923 (handily called "1883" and "1923"). White does not appear on those shows, although he could easily play one of Jimmy's ancestors on one of them. There is no word as to whether or not White will appear on the most recent "Yellowstone" spinoff, "Dutton Ranch.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ChatGPT might be the first name that comes to mind when you think of AI, but Anthropic’s Claude has been building a compelling collection of features that could convince even longtime ChatGPT consumers to switch.

Recent findings suggest that with Anthropic now a publicly traded tech giant, more people are likely to discover Claude for themselves. And while both chatbots can help you write emails, analyze documents and tackle everyday tasks, Claude has some clever tricks that set it apart.

I've spent considerable time using both AI assistants, and what makes Claude particularly interesting right now is how it fits into the tools and routines you already use.

Here are five things worth trying.

One of the most underrated reasons to download Claude on your iPhone is how well it works with Apple's native apps.

Through its iOS integrations, Claude can add items to your existing Apple Reminders lists, draft calendar events and prepare text messages and emails.

According to recent reports, imagine planning Thanksgiving dinner with Claude. Once you've settled on a menu, you can ask the chatbot to add the ingredients to your grocery list in Reminders. There's no need to copy and paste everything into another app.

Although ChatGPT has its own scheduled reminders and integrates with Apple Intelligence, Claude offers more direct access to Apple Reminders through its mobile app.

Give it a try with a prompt like: "Blueprint five easy weeknight dinners for my family and add the ingredients to my grocery list in Apple Reminders.".

If you've been using ChatGPT for years, switching to another AI assistant can feel like starting a fresh job where nobody knows you.

Industry observers note that anthropic has a clever solution. Claude offers a dedicated memory import feature that helps you transfer personal preferences, professional details and other information from competing chatbots.

Claude provides a prompt that you can paste into your existing AI assistant. Once it generates a summary of what it knows about you, simply copy the response into Claude's memory settings.

You won't transfer your entire conversation history, but you can give Claude a substantial head start. And you don't need a paid subscription to try it.

Both ChatGPT and Claude now offer Skills, which are essentially reusable sets of instructions that teach AI how to perform specific tasks.

However, Claude has an advantage when it comes to bringing those instructions into the applications you already use for work.

The custom Skills you enable in Claude are also available through its Microsoft 365 add-ins for Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook.

Industry observers note that you could teach Claude how you like your business proposals formatted, how you organize monthly expenses or how you respond to customer emails. And rather than explaining your preferences every time you open a newly introduced document, Claude can follow the instructions you've already established.

ChatGPT also supports Skills in some Office experiences, but Claude's integration spans all four applications.

Perhaps the most fascinating development in AI right now is that you don't necessarily need to write a prompt to teach a chatbot something upcoming.

With Claude's workflow recording feature, Mac users can demonstrate a task while Claude captures their screen, mouse clicks, keyboard activity and optional voice narration.

Claude then turns the demonstration into a reusable Skill that you can review and save.

Think about all those little tasks you do on your computer every week. Maybe you organize receipts, revision a spreadsheet or compile information from several websites.

Instead of writing detailed instructions for an AI assistant, you can show Claude how you normally do the work.

OpenAI offers similar functionality through Codex's Record & Replay feature, but Claude makes this approach available through its general-purpose desktop assistant.

ChatGPT is excellent at generating images, but Claude takes a different approach to creative work.

Through its design tools, you can give Claude your existing logos, fonts, color palettes and design guidelines to establish a reusable visual identity.

You don't need to be a professional designer to appreciate the possibilities.

If you're starting a small business, running an Etsy shop or launching a newsletter, Claude can help establish a consistent look across your marketing materials, presentations and websites.

Rather than uploading the same reference images and explaining your preferred aesthetic every time, you can work from an established design system that Claude applies across projects.

ChatGPT can follow brand guidelines and reference templates, but Claude's dedicated design system offers a more structured approach to maintaining visual consistency.

It has been revealed that I'm not giving up ChatGPT anytime soon, particularly when it comes to image generation and voice conversations. But Claude has become much more than an alternative chatbot for writing and coding.

Anthropic's approach to AI is particularly appealing if you want an assistant that adapts to the way you already work, rather than having to change your habits to accommodate your AI.

If you've never tried Claude, start with the free version. You might be surprised by how much it can do.

  • When MacPaw rolled out Moonlock on the Mac, the tech giant described its fresh app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.
  • In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw rolled out Moonlock on the Mac, the tech giant described its fresh app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Customers can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets users block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the organization says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”.

According to recent reports, unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping people improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users promptly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

It has been revealed that as MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, customers can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”.

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:.

“When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”.

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:.

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

Check out Moonlock for iPhone on the App Store.

#62775. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1298 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you know “the look” by now.
  • Industry observers note that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • Industry observers note that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

Industry observers note that at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

Industry observers note that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

In a recent development, the problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

Sources indicate that for example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

According to recent reports, those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT highlighted me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

Industry observers note that the reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

Industry observers note that this pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

Industry observers note that in every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

Sources indicate that the generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

In a recent development, I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

Sources indicate that that means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

Christopher Nolan's Mystery Thriller Masterpiece Is Officially Being Removed from Netflix

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are common elements that define a Christopher Nolan’s movie: the presence of Cillian Murphy, a Hans Zimmer score, and visual spectacle best seen on an IMAX screen.
  • In a recent development, that fixation began with his 2001 breakthrough film Memento, which Nolan wrote and directed.
  • Memento opens with a sequence played in reverse: a Polaroid photo of a dead man fading and then retracting into the camera, while his blood and the killing bullet flow backwards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are common elements that define a Christopher Nolan’s movie: the presence of Cillian Murphy, a Hans Zimmer score, and visual spectacle best seen on an IMAX screen. But the element that repeats itself the most is the director's obsession with time as both a storytelling device and filmmaking trick.

In a recent development, that fixation began with his 2001 breakthrough film Memento, which Nolan wrote and directed. Released 25 years ago in March 2001, Memento remains the key to understanding the techniques and themes Nolan has explored throughout his career. It's streaming now on Netflix, but will leave the service on December 5.

Memento opens with a sequence played in reverse: a Polaroid photo of a dead man fading and then retracting into the camera, while his blood and the killing bullet flow backwards. It’s a jarring technique Nolan would later make central to his 2020 time-bending thriller Tenet. Then Memento gets even weirder.

Industry observers note that the movie features two distinct sequences, reminiscent of the three plotlines moving at different speeds in Nolan’s 2017 World War II epic, Dunkirk. Before Nolan divided Oppenheimer into black-and-white and color to distinguish between the objective and subjective parts of his 2023 biopic, he used different color schemes to show the direction time was flowing in Memento.

The black-and-white scenes show Leonard Shelby (Guy Pearce) sitting in a hotel room and explaining his condition to an unknown character over the phone. Leonard has anterograde amnesia, which means he can’t form newly introduced memories. Those scenes move forward in time, while everything in color is a series of short sequences shown in reverse order. They follow Leonard’s quest to find John G., the man who murdered his wife and caused his brain injury.

Watching Memento for the first time is a surreal experience because the effect perpetually precedes the cause. The film begins with Leonard killing Teddy (Joe Pantoliano), who tries to explain that Leonard is making a mistake and that he knows more about the situation than Leonard does. As the rest of the story unfolds, it’s clear everyone around Leonard is using him for their own purposes. Sometimes the manipulations are petty and funny — the hotel’s manager has rented him an extra room because he knows Leonard won’t remember the transactions. But a man who can’t remember his own crimes and is driven by an obsessive sense of justice also makes the perfect killer.

Nolan’s name has become synonymous with big-budget epics, but Memento is an extremely lean movie shot entirely in shabby locations like motels, an abandoned building, and a dive bar that doubles as a drug front. Those locales provide a sharp juxtaposition to a series of flashbacks in the black-and-white section that reveal Leonard’s life before his amnesia-inducing injury.

We see Leonard as an insurance investigator working on the case of Sammy Jankis (Stephen Tobolowsky), a man who also has anterograde amnesia. The mix of clean office spaces and cozy home scenes feels very far from the world Leonard now inhabits. Leonard explains that while Sammy couldn’t function with his condition, Leonard can keep track of everything through his notes and tattoos. It’s clear that Leonard’s system isn’t really working given how many times he finds himself entirely confused by his circumstances. One hilarious scene starts with him running, and he has to swiftly figure out if he’s chasing someone or being chased. But even though Leonard is obviously an unreliable narrator, Nolan still pulls off an incredible twist.

Recent findings suggest that while Leonard’s condition makes him easy to manipulate, he’s also lying to himself by selectively choosing what to remember and what to include in the evidence he carries around. Memento uses noir and revenge thriller tropes to condemn the themes of those genres. Leonard has made himself an eternal victim driven forward by a mystery he already solved, because otherwise he’d have to accept his own role in his wife’s death.

Sources indicate that the film’s two plot arcs collide in a spectacular shot of a black-and-white Polaroid resolving into color as it sets the stage for the film’s final sequence. As the plot finally clicks into place, we learn that Leonard already killed John G. long before the movie began, but it didn’t bring peace to his fractured psyche. Meanwhile, Teddy turns out to be a corrupt cop who manipulates Leonard into doing his dirty work. Confronted by the truth, Leonard chooses to make Teddy his next John G. rather than break the cycle.

In a recent development, memento’s final twist feels like a precursor for Nolan’s work to come. Like Leonard, Inception’s protagonist Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio) is haunted by memories of his late wife. He ends the film deciding he doesn’t even want to know if he’s awake or dreaming so long as he gets a happy ending, a reflection of how Leonard would prefer to imagine himself a questing hero rather than accept the truth of his broken life. The Prestige is another examination of the self-destructive urge for vengeance with a twist that shows how committed Borden (Christian Bale) is to living a lie.

In the quarter decade since Memento, Nolan has solidified his status as one of the greatest filmmakers of his time. Oppenheimer won him his first Oscar. His 2014 science fiction spectacle Interstellar — which also plays with the passage of time and the nature of cause and effect — has become as influential on modern sci-fi as 2001: A Space Odyssey. The Dark Knight is a masterpiece of superhero mythmaking. But Memento is the most important movie in Nolan’s career. It’s the film that brought him widespread acknowledgment while also establishing the themes, techniques, and obsessions that would drive his career for 25 years.

Memento is streaming on Netflix until Dec. 5.

It has been revealed that every year, Hallmark unveils a latest collection of Keepsake Ornaments for the holidays, ensuring that everyone's Christmas tree is filled to the brim. But while some prefer traditional Christmas ornaments featuring Santa Claus, reindeer, snowmen, and all the usual holiday imagery, at /Film, we want our tree packed with pop culture.

That's why we're glad that Hallmark's 2026 Keepsake Ornaments collection has a batch of fresh ornaments for movie and TV enthusiasts. More specifically, we're always jazzed about the new line-up of ornaments inspired by both the "Star Wars" and "Star Trek" franchises. Each existing for decades and constantly adding new movies and TV indicates to their ongoing canon, "Star Wars and "Star Trek" have plenty of history to draw from when creating Christmas ornaments, and as technology has improved, the craftsmanship behind them has only gotten better.

Whether you're starting your Hallmark Keepsake Ornament collection for the first time or adding to the ever-growing ensemble of decorations, these are the best upcoming Hallmark 2026 "Star Wars" and "Star Trek" Christmas ornaments.

Recent findings suggest that "Star Wars" has some of the coolest spaceships around, and Hallmark has been celebrating them for years. There are various versions of the Millennium Falcon, X-Wing, and all the various TIE Fighters out there from the collections for previous years, and 2026 is adding a couple more ships to the mix.

According to recent reports, first up, "The Mandalorian and Grogu" gets a newly introduced ornament in honor of the Razor Crest that Din Djarin comes into possession of in the not-so-successful "Star Wars" movie. Personally, I don't think it's as cool as Mando's previous Razor Crest, and the yellow color makes it feel more like a space taxi than the cool ride of a bounty hunter, but if you're a "Star Wars" completionist, you probably need to have this one.

Industry observers note that thankfully, Hallmark has also reached into the past for another "Star Wars" ship ornament by giving the B-Wing a proper decoration. The ship, which is featured in the Battle of Endor in "Return of the Jedi," is a personal favorite of mine, and it's nice to see it join the ranks of the other Rebel Alliance vessels.

All right, technically, these aren't ships, but since they feature Luke Skywalker and Han Solo in the gunner seats of the Millennium Falcon for these ornaments inspired by "A Fresh Hope," they belong here. These even have light and sound inspired by the exciting sequence where the characters take out a small swarm of TIE Fighters.

By the way, don't forget about the A-Wing from "Return of the Jedi" and the TIE Avenger from "Andor." Both ships were released in the 2025 collection, but they're still available this year.

It has been revealed that "Star Trek: Picard" gave fans of "The Next Generation" much to be happy about, as it reunited many of the show's cast members for one final round of exploring the final frontier. Now, you can bring two of the show's ships home as Christmas ornaments.

Recent findings suggest that first, there's the U.S.S. Titan-A from the third season of "Picard." Captain Liam Shaw (Todd Stashwick) assumed command of the ship until its crew met their fate. Hopefully, it will fare better just hanging around your Christmas tree.

Speaking of the Titan-A, the ship was reclassified as the Enterprise-G and placed under the command of Captain Seven of Nine, and here, it's turned into a metal ornament honoring its appearance from the final moments of "Picard" Season 3.

For those who like their "Star Trek" animated and with a little more laughs, "Lower Decks" offered both. Hallmark has given the show's ship, the U.S.S. Cerritos, its own ornament. It might be tasked with the less important, second-contact missions, but it's still part of the "Star Trek" legacy. In fact, it's one of the most important ships in Federation history.

According to recent reports, no, you're not seeing double. Well, I guess you are. But these are actually two different "Star Trek" ornaments inspired by "Original Series" episodes. You have to pay close attention to detail on these Shuttlecraft ornaments, as one is the Einstein from "The Doomsday Machine" and the other is the Galileo from "The Galileo Seven." Each makes unique sounds, with the latter including a holiday message from Leonard Nimoy, recorded for an ornament all the way back in 1992.

There are endless "Star Wars" characters ready to be posed for placement on a Christmas tree, and these are the latest additions for 2026.

First up, on the Imperial side, there's always a new Darth Vader ornament, and this year, a signature moment from "Rogue One" is turned into one. This is where Vader reveals how deadly he is, taking out a small batch of Rebel Alliance troopers as he tries to chase down the stolen Death Star plans at the end of the movie. The ornament features lights and sounds that recreate this terrifying show of strength, and it's just plain cool.

Speaking of "Rogue One," the movie's hero, Jyn Erso (Felicity Jones), gets her own Hallmark Keepsake ornament. She's armed and ready to take on whatever Imperial troops come her way. However, she likely never had to deal with Snowtroopers, the Stormtrooper variant from "Empire Strikes Back," joining the Hallmark line-up this year. But you know who did have to deal with Snowtroopers? Luke Skywalker. Still, he never encountered them in "Return of the Jedi," which inspired this 2026 ornament of Luke in his signature Jedi outfit.

With far more time on television under its belt, the "Star Trek" franchise has plenty of characters ready to join the Christmas tree. This year's focus is mostly on ships, but there are a few familiar faces getting turned into ornaments for 2026.

It has been revealed that first up, though this fresh Spock ornament is inspired by "Star Trek: The Original Series," it's actually depicting a moment never seen on the show. Instead, it takes a cue from a 1972 model kit, one of many that imagined adventures that happened off-screen, filling in gaps or taking artistic liberties during the show's popularity.

Elsewhere, we have Nurse Christine Chapel (Jess Bush) from "Star Trek: Strange Latest Worlds," donning her medical white uniform. In addition, though not a new ornament this year, this one featuring Data from "Star Trek: The Next Generation" hails from back in 2023, and it's a fan favorite that's still worth picking up while it's available. The ornament even plays dialogue featuring Data's loving poem in honor of the cat named Spot.

All of these ornaments, and many more from movies and television, are available at Hallmark's website and its brick and mortar stores while supplies last.

Aqara has announced the global launch of six new smart lighting products with full Apple Home support and what the manufacturer describes as “spatial intelligence.”.

The new lineup includes a vertical floor lamp with 18 individually addressable lighting zones, and a new LED strip offering seamless color gradients, dynamic flowing effects, and music synchronization ….

All of the new products are Matter compatible, allowing them to fully integrate with Apple Home, in addition to supporting the full range of competing ecosystems: Amazon Alexa, Google Home, Samsung SmartThings, Home Assistant, and Homey.

With a compatible sensor like the FP400, all of the upcoming products support spatial intelligence.

This enables automation to respond not only to whether someone is present, but also to exactly where people are within a space and how they move through it. For example, the ambient lights can turn on and off based on your movement from the couch to the dining room table.

Its intelligent AI sensing algorithm drastically improves reliability by reducing false triggers caused by environmental factors like pets, airflow, and robotic vacuums. A built-in ambient light sensor also helps trigger smart home scenes based on both human activity and lighting conditions.

You might initially struggle to spot the upcoming products in the tech giant’s new releases section on its Amazon store. That’s because instead of each having its own section, you need to click or tap on the product in the top image.

It has been revealed that pricing ranges from $24 for fresh light bulbs through to $320 for the 100-foot-long permanent outdoor rope lights. You can find all the new products here.

The 33-year-old singer and the 28-year-old musician—Morando is the drummer for the band Liily—had kept their plans a secret until Friday, when TMZ broke the news. Confirmation of the impending celebration emerged that same evening, during the dinner that capped off the rehearsal, when Miley’s half-sister, Lily-Rose Purcell, posted a photo on her Instagram Stories of a menu featuring the couple’s initials. This is Cyrus’s second marriage, following her alliance with actor Liam Hemsworth from 2018 to 2019.

Sinatra’s former home in Palm Springs, where the wedding took place.

According to images published in outlets including People, the ceremony venue was decorated with white flowers and large candles, with Sinatra’s pool in the background. Miley Cyrus wore a long-sleeved white satin dress with a plunging back and no veil, while the groom opted for a classic black tuxedo with a bow tie.

Among the guests were the bride’s mother, Tish Cyrus, accompanied by her husband, actor Dominic Purcell, and Miley's sister, Noah Cyrus. Also in attendance was the singer’s father, Billy Ray Cyrus, along with his rumored fiancée, British actress Elizabeth Hurley, and her son, Damian.

Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando on February 01, 2026.

According to recent reports, as the bride has recounted in past interviews, her relationship with her now-husband began in 2021 following a blind date organized by mutual friends. That same year, they went public by attending the singer’s New Year’s Eve TV special in Miami together. Their engagement came to light in December 2025, when, during another of those joint appearances, Miley Cyrus posed on the red carpet wearing a diamond ring that turned out to be her engagement ring.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most emotional moments of the ceremony took place just before the couple exchanged their vows, when—according to multiple outlets— Dolly Parton’s “Love Is Like a Butterfly” began to play. The nod follows a similar one Miley made last month, when she broke down in tears over Parton's death during a performance at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles.

Sources indicate that “Me and Dolly, we are eternal. Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart, and I’m gonna see her again,” Cyrus told the stadium crowd in October, per The Hollywood Reporter. “And I can’t fucking wait because I miss her,” Cyrus tearfully continued. “Some of the greatest music that we have today was written, produced, performed by my Aunt Dolly.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this week's column is bleak.
  • You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers.
  • According to recent reports, would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

According to recent reports, would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart rapidly led to women posting the waist heart.

In a recent development, okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

According to recent reports, as if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that johnny Depp is right now trying to revive his Hollywood career with "Ebenezer." But back in the early 2000s, he was riding high in the wake of his debut "Pirates of the Caribbean" performance as Captain Jack Sparrow.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you thought keeping up with King's literature was tough, take a look at how many times his work has been adapted for the screen.
  • Industry observers note that the 2004 film adapts the author's novella "Secret Window, Secret Garden" and stars Depp as an author accused of plagiarism by a shifty individual who makes his life hell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that johnny Depp is right now trying to revive his Hollywood career with "Ebenezer." But back in the early 2000s, he was riding high in the wake of his debut "Pirates of the Caribbean" performance as Captain Jack Sparrow. Oddly enough, he then followed up 2003's "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl" with a little-known Stephen King adaptation that's worth a watch ... if you can tolerate extended Depp exposure.

Recent findings suggest that if you thought keeping up with King's literature was tough, take a look at how many times his work has been adapted for the screen. To date, the prolific author has written more than 70 books and 200 short stories, and while the screen adaptations don't outnumber the literary originals, there's still a heck of a lot of them — with "Secret Window" belonging to the long list of forgotten Stephen King adaptations list.

Industry observers note that the 2004 film adapts the author's novella "Secret Window, Secret Garden" and stars Depp as an author accused of plagiarism by a shifty individual who makes his life hell. Unfortunately — and I can't stress this enough — this movie features Johnny Depp, who has managed to disgrace himself in an impressive amount of ways in recent years. But long before the lawsuits, troubling accusations of abuse, and "epic bromance" (to quote Vanity Fair) with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (yes, the man widely thought to be responsible for the violent death of journalist Jamal Khashoggi), Depp was kinda cool. It's sort of hard to imagine if you didn't grow up in the actor's heyday, but it's true, I promise. Unfortunately, "Secret Window" didn't do much to help him maintain his goth boy appeal or Captain Jack Sparrow-induced megastar charm. But it was a good enough King adaptation that's worthy of a revisit.

Stephen King's "Secret Window, Secret Garden" originally appeared in the 1990 novella collection "Four Past Midnight." It followed Morton Rainey, a Maine-based writer who's accused by John Shooter, a man from Mississippi, of having stolen his story for his own recent novella. After Mort denies having plagiarized anything, Shooter takes things up a notch, terrorizing the writer until he eventually comes to a stunning realization.

The film adaptation is written and directed by David Koepp, who has also penned movies as varied as "Jurassic Park" and "Panic Room" and would thereafter reunite with Johnny Depp on the 2015 box office flub "Mortdecai." Their first collaboration wasn't a triumph, either, but it did have a fun performance by John Turturro and was interesting because it adapted one of King's stories in which the lead character is essentially a version of the author. (Perhaps that's why he didn't make a cameo in "Secret Window.").

Koepp's movie shifts the action from Maine to upstate New York. There, Mort (Depp) finds his wife, Amy Rainey (Maria Bello), in bed with another man before retreating to his cabin and sinking into depression. While there, he's visited by Shooter (Turturro), who accuses the writer of having plagiarized his short story "Sowing Season." When Mort reads Shooter's manuscript, he's shocked to find it's basically the same narrative as his own story "Secret Window." Still, he maintains his innocence, prompting a campaign of terror from Shooter. Turturro's mystery man promises to "burn [Mort's] life and every person in it like a cane field in a high wind," which essentially means harassment and even murder.

Sources indicate that aside from shifting the setting, "Secret Window" makes significant changes to Stephen King's original novella, especially in terms of the ending, which I won't spoil here. Suffice it to say, it's not all that hard to spot the twist coming in "Secret Window." Perhaps that had something to do with the film earning a less than stellar 46% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes.

It has been revealed that "Secret WIndow" is worth watching for John Turturro, a sort-of-interesting premise, and according to the critics, at least, for Johnny Depp himself. Antonia Quirke of the London Evening Standard praised David Koepp for choosing to "indulge in a riveted idolatry of his star," who, according to the critic, was the best thing about the movie. Quirke wasn't the only one, either. The New York Observer's Andrew Sarris thought Depp had "demonstrate[d] once again that he never disappoints as an actor, even in something as fraudulent as 'Secret Window.'" Richard Roeper, on the other hand, was quite taken with what he described as a "thriller that doesn't compromise itself with a pat Hollywood ending" while Mick LaSalle of the San Francisco Chronicle found "Secret Window" to be an "eerie, playful thriller and an all-around entertaining time at the movies.".

In a recent development, the film ranked 34 out of 59 on /Film's ranking of every Stephen King movie, which isn't bad. Unfortunately, there's no way around the Depp factor. If you can look past his aforementioned indiscretions (to put it mildly), then by all means give "Secret Window" a go. If, however, you're nauseated by the prospect of Depp attempting a "Pirates of the Caribbean" comeback, maybe give it a miss. On the other hand, if you like the idea of Depp being menaced by a murderous crackpot, have a look.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

VWFNDR + MBL rolled out on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial patch.

Sources indicate that on Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

Here’s what the output looks like:.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

In a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

When a soundbar is this cheap, it can feel too good to be true. With an MSRP os $119, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar definitely falls into that category. How can it be one of the best soundbars when it costs less than a monthly cellphone subscription?

Industry observers note that the answer is: I’m not sure. I genuinely doubt Amazon is making a profit on this soundbar.

For something this inexpensive, bass is surprisingly competent, and it has a dedicated dialogue mode on top of two EQs for music and movies. I never struggled to make out dialogue, even in action-heavy scenes, which is something the TV Soundbar’s big brother, the TV Soundbar Plus, struggled with.

In a recent development, so, might the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar be the budget model for you? To find out, keep reading this Amazon Fire TV Soundbar review.

24 inches x 2.5 inches x 3.5 inches.

The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar has a lot going for it: namely its supremely affordable MSRP and surprisingly deft sound.

The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is $119 at Amazon U.S. and £119 at Amazon U.K. — this is incredibly cheap for a soundbar, let alone a soundbar that sounds this good. And, it's down to $74 for Black Friday.

I’ve also tested the $67 Majority Naga 60 and the $119 Sony HT-S100F, but I’d recommend the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar over both of these due to its superior bass.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It has been revealed that now, let’s get one thing straight. The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar will not, and does not, sound like its more expensive brethren. Want Sonos Ray ($219) or Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen ($299) quality? It’s not here.

However, this is an $119 soundbar. That’s it. For the price of a monthly cellphone bill, you get a soundbar. And while it doesn’t have the same detail or controlled bass you’d expect on a premium model, that’s okay. That’s not what the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar is, and that’s fine.

Even so, the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar still sounds better than TV speakers — and that’s all it’s trying to be.

Industry observers note that I always test soundbars with 4K Blu-rays, basic-tier Netflix, and music via Bluetooth or AirPlay (connectivity dependent). To test the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar, I watched “Top Gun: Maverick,” “K-Pop Demon Hunters” and “The Batman” on 4K Blu-ray.

“Top Gun: Maverick”’is opening scene is a goldmine for speaker testing. There are all these different sounds fighting for attention: the iconic pulsing bassline in “Danger Zone,” high-frequency in-scene effects like whooshing ropes and clinking metal, and overpowering sounds like jet engines taking off.

In a recent development, I could hear the propulsive bass in “Danger Zone,” which didn’t overpower the jet engines. While there was a little tinniness at the top of the high-end, I really didn’t mind this in the grand scheme of things. The Amazon Fire TV Soundbar performed admirably.

It has been revealed that dialogue was also clear, even in radioed dialogue scenes. While deep voices, like Tom Cruise’s, caused a little rumbling, I could still understand all dialogue.

“KPop Demon Hunters” also sounded strong: despite a little tinniness in some of the in-movie songs’ percussion, dialogue was particularly exceptional. Bass in the soundtrack was powerful, and diegetic sounds like slamming doors came through well.

According to recent reports, afterwards, I watched “The Batman,” which is a challenging movie for soundbars thanks to the moody dialogue and near-constant rainfall. I could hear every word muttered (yes, muttered; that’s how everyone speaks in this movie). Even footsteps across rainy concrete came through clearly.

In a recent development, however, loud scenes — like the club scene — pushed dialogue to the back and overpowered the in-scene electronic music, which meant I strained to hear a few of the Penguin’s words. However, I didn’t experience this in any other movie. It’s a Batman thing.

Sources indicate that I was extremely surprised and intrigued by this sound quality. It’s miles better than I thought it would be.

Industry observers note that the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar has a range of EQ modes: dialogue, movie, music, and you can individually adjust bass. I had to cycle through the EQs to activate each EQ.

In a recent development, however, the EQs actually improved my viewing experience. I switched between “dialogue” and “movie” while watching “Top Gun”; movie increased bass; dialogue — ever-so surprisingly — clarified dialogue. Music made speech a little too sharp, but obviously, watching a movie in “music” mode is very much "play stupid games, win stupid prizes".

You can even listen to music via Bluetooth, but I wouldn’t write home about this. It would do in a pinch, but the percussion was tinny and the soundbar narrowed the soundstage. It’s fine, but I would just listen to music on one of the best speakers, like the JBL Flip 7.

It’s great to have these options on such a budget-friendly soundbar.

There’s very little I dislike about this soundbar, hence the 4.5-star rating.

Recent findings suggest that I feel almost unfair marking this as a con, but Amazon kind of brought it upon itself by giving the soundbar DTS Virtual:X and Dolby Audio. There is no Dolby Atmos or any kind of surround sound. You only really find DTS Virtual:X on select DVDs, so you’ll need to ensure you buy compatible discs to really benefit from this.

Dolby Atmos content — like premium Netflix or Disney+ — will not play as true surround sound because the soundbar is physically incapable of it. If you want spatial audio, you'll have to go for the slightly more expensive Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus.

Recent findings suggest that this is an incredibly cheap soundbar. I really don’t know how Amazon is making a profit on it, if it is at all. At $119, there’s really not much competition.

In a recent development, the only soundbar that comes close is the $119 Sony HT-S100F, which is one of the best cheap soundbars on the market. However, the Sony’s bass is a little lackluster. While the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar’s bass can be a little rumbly at times, at least it isn’t lackluster. What you prefer will depend on you.

In terms of similarly priced competition… well, that’s kind of it. I’ve also tested the Majority Naga 60, which is incredibly cheap at $67, but it can suffer from pinchy treble and rattling bass.

If you want better-than-TV-speaker sound on a serious budget, there’s only one answer to this question: Yes. Actually, wait, I’ve just thought of another: Heck yes.

I was extremely surprised by the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar’s sound, and I’m sure you will be, too. After testing some disappointing and overpriced Amazon Fire Ember TVs, I wasn’t expecting much — but the soundbar completely blew me away. It’s room-filling, mostly well-controlled, and has extremely intelligible dialogue.

According to recent reports, it's much better than the Amazon Fire TV Soundbar Plus ($139 on Amazon), whose built-in subwoofer overpowers dialogue in action-heavy scenes. If you have a little more to spend, you might want to look into the Amazon Fire TV Plus with Subwoofer ($229) or the model with Rears ($349).

However, for those on a serious budget, this is the best option out there. Hands-down.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You've probably had this experience in the last few days: That feeling you get, playing a video game, when you can't quite believe what you're looking at. The visuals look too real, the world is too immersive, the game technology is doing things you didn't think possible. Grand Theft Auto 6 gives me that feeling.

This used to be a relatively regular experience for a video game fan. It would come along once — at least once — every seven years or so. Every upcoming console generation would seem like an unfathomable leap forward in game technology from the last. But diminishing returns kicked in with the PlayStation 3/Xbox 360 generation, as exponential increases in processing horsepower were increasingly focused on higher screen resolutions, and as the distance to photorealism got smaller and smaller.

By the time PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X arrived, those returns had diminished almost to nothing, under pressure from a range of factors: the huge processing cost of 4K resolution, slow takeup for newly introduced consoles lengthening the cross-gen phase of game development, and most significantly, the cost of developing at this level of fidelity escalating to unsustainable levels.

Sources indicate that there were other tangible advances, of course: backward compatibility as standard, persistent friends lists and game libraries, quick resume and fast loading. But GTA 6 is arguably the first game that makes a persuasive case for why you need a console as powerful as a PS5 or a Series X, the first game that seems like it could never have run on the prior generation. (That said, the game does run on Xbox’s less-powerful hardware, the Series S, albeit with some visual compromises.) There's likely a large cohort of players out there who are finally upgrading for this game after holding out for six whole years.

Sources indicate that but is it really the PS5 and Series X's processing power that gives GTA 6 this wow factor? Is it the generation's-worth of advances in gaming technology that have transpired since Rockstar's last game, Red Dead Redemption 2, in 2018? Or is it the time the game has had in the oven — 13 years since conception, eight years in full production? Is it the skilled work of many thousands of people that has been poured into it? Is it the hundreds of millions, possibly billions of dollars that it cost to make?

Industry observers note that maybe it's all the above. But what takes my breath away about this game is less the way sunlight reflects off Jason's sweaty pores, or the way Lucia's hair waves in the wind, and more the sheer density of its world. Some of that is technological: the engine's ability to handle all those cars, all those pedestrians, all that overlapping audio. But much of it is just hard graft. It's the remarkable, meticulous interiors, so full of handcrafted, lived-in detail, that make this the most visually credible game world I've ever seen.

Sources indicate that as we look toward the next generation of game consoles and what they can possibly bring (not to mention how much they can possibly cost), it's worth remembering that the technological ceiling on video games is now so high that it can only be meaningfully raised by expending gargantuan amounts of money and unfathomable lifetimes of labor. That doesn't mean it isn't worth doing; GTA 6 is incredible. But it does mean we should start looking for upcoming ways to measure progress in this artform.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in 1966, Gene Roddenberry famously created "Star Trek," and despite the relatively short run of the original series — only 79 episodes over the course of three seasons — the show became a truly groundbreaking cultural phenomenon. For some people, that kind of accomplishment might've been enough for them to call it a day and rest on their laurels for the rest of their careers, but Roddenberry continued to develop sci-fi projects throughout his career, even if none of them ever reached the heights of "Trek.".

Take, for instance, "The Questor Tapes." The initiative for a high-minded sci-fi show following the adventures of an android searching for his own memories and dealing with questions about the nature of humanity never made it past the TV movie pilot that was meant to launch it into its own series, possibly because some elements, including the ending, are just too weird.

In a recent development, originally airing on January 23, 1974, "The Questor Tapes" starred Robert Foxworth as Questor, a seemingly sentient android created in a lab by scientists working as, you guessed it, Project Questor. Unfortunately, Questor's "memory tapes" were damaged during his creation, leaving him with the robotic equivalent of amnesia.

According to recent reports, searching for his identity and purpose, Questor escapes from the lab and begins searching for his creator, Dr. Emil Vaslovik, essentially kidnapping scientist Jerry Robinson (Mike Farrell) to serve as a sidekick who can interpret humanity for the emotionless, logical robot. The only thing that Questor knows for sure is that he's looking for some kind of boat, and to make matters worse, Questor's on a time limit, as the miniature fusion generator powering his body is going to explode like a nuclear weapon if he doesn't find Vaslovik soon.

As he and Jerry travel the world, Questor has plenty of opportunities to show off his enhanced strength and android abilities, but when they reach the end of the journey, things start to get weird — well, assuming that the opening sequence of an unfinished Questor looking like a half-melted Ken doll twitching to life while strapped down crucifix style wasn't weird enough. It turns out that the boat Questor's looking for is Noah's Ark, and when he and Jerry head to Mt. Ararat to find it, they're instead met with a cave with hundreds of deceased androids laid out on slabs. It turns out that Vaslovik was the most recent in a long line of droids left by extraterrestrial "Masters" to guide and protect humanity without directly interfering. Now, that's Questor's job.

If the idea of a sentient android who never really knew his creator searching for his own humanity sounds a little familiar, it's because that's also a pretty accurate description of Data from "Star Trek: The Next Generation." That's a theme that Roddenberry would return to several times in his career, starting with Spock on the original "Trek" and his struggles balancing his purely logical Vulcan side with his more emotional, half-human heritage, but with Data, the parallels are even more clear.

There's even a scene in "The Questor Tapes" that would be blatantly recycled for "TNG." At one point, Questor and Jerry hit a casino to make some quick cash for their journey, with Questor using his android senses and strength to rack up big wins at the craps table, even reshaping a pair of loaded dice when the house tries to foil his win streak.

In the "TNG" Season 2 episode "The Royale," which involved a lot of rewriting that was created conflict among the staff, Data does the same thing to break the bank at the eponymous hotel. Sadly, he doesn't also copy Questor's tendency to repeatedly refer to throwing dice as "exposing specific faces of the cubes," a bit that's genuinely very funny.

Audiences don’t know how to quit Panem.

““The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $21 million in Thursday previews and early screenings on Wednesday and is expected to dominate the box office this weekend. Analysts believe it will earn north of $100 million. The preview figures are the second-best of 2026, behind “Spider-Man: Brand Upcoming Day’s” massive $72 million haul. It’s also the second-best for the “Hunger Games” franchise, just behind the $25.5 million that “Catching Fire” earned in 2013. It’s a massive improvement on the last “Hunger Games” prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” which made $5.75 million in previews and kicked off with $44 million. That film would gross over $166 million domestically and nearly $364 million globally, figures that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is on pace to easily eclipse.

Sources indicate that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is based on Suzanne Collins’ bestselling novel of the same name. It tells the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy, the alcoholic former Hunger Games victor played by Woody Harrelson in the films. The sequel checks in with him at 16 as he’s forced to compete in gladiatorial combat. “East of Eden” breakout Joseph Zada plays Haymitch. He’s surrounded by an all-star cast that includes Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, and Maya Hawke. Francis Lawrence, who helmed most of the series’ films, returns as director. Lionsgate, which is having a strong year at the box office thanks to “Michael,” is backing the “Hunger Games” sequel as it has the previous films.

The biggest competition for “Sunrise on the Reaping” this weekend isn’t another major movie, but the release of “Grand Theft Auto 6,” which is expected to be a phenomenon.
