All 10 James Bond Movies Not Based On Ian Fleming's Books, Ranked

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we're taking a look back at the James Bond movies that are not based on Ian Fleming's books and short stories.
  • Here are all 10 James Bond movies not based on Ian Fleming's books ranked, going in their own direction with the super-spy.
  • Pierce Brosnan at the moment remains the only actor whose entire run as James Bond featured original narratives for his movies, rather than drawing directly from a specific Fleming story.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we're taking a look back at the James Bond movies that are not based on Ian Fleming's books and short stories. Some of the entries here take their titles from short stories written by Ian Fleming but, frankly, nothing else. Outside of the inclusion of Bond and his usual allies and enemies, these cinematic narratives really strike out on their own creatively.

Here are all 10 James Bond movies not based on Ian Fleming's books ranked, going in their own direction with the super-spy.

Pierce Brosnan at the moment remains the only actor whose entire run as James Bond featured original narratives for his movies, rather than drawing directly from a specific Fleming story. In taking Bond out of the Cold War setting in which he originated, this led to an uneven tenure, despite Brosnan's best efforts. However, nothing could quite save Brosnan's last turn as 007 in 2002's "Die Another Day," opening with a title track by Madonna that sounded dated when it was released. The movie has Bond square off with a rogue North Korean general while trying to identify who betrayed him on a mission that led to a prolonged torturous imprisonment.

IMDb names "Die Another Day" as the worst James Bond movie, a dubious distinction that is, unfortunately, well-deserved. The movie opens with Bond infiltrating North Korea by surfing, because that's clearly what the kids are still into, and it only gets worse from there. This backslide into mediocrity spreads to the cinematography, complete with shoddy CG effects and random slow-motion sequences for no discernible reason other than an attempt to look cool. An absolute travesty and an embarrassing way for Brosnan to end his time as Bond, "Die Another Day" is a grating viewing experience.

Yes, "A View to a Kill," Moore's swan song to the franchise, takes its title from the 1960 Fleming short story "From a View to a Kill." But whereas the literary namesake features Bond hunting a motorcycle-driving assassin in France, the 1985 movie pits 007 against an immoral tech tycoon before it was cool. The tycoon in question is Max Zorin (Christopher Walken), a sadistic figure looking to corner the microchip market by destroying Silicon Valley. But outside of Walken chewing the scenery, joined by Grace Jones playing his enforcer, and a memorable title track by Duran Duran, the movie falls flat.

Sources indicate that roger Moore was horrified by "A View to a Kill," particularly the widespread casual violence, as Zorin mercilessly murders many of his associates. We're personally horrified by how rough around the edges the overall movie is, from its lackluster stunts to its abrupt finale. To make matters worse, when the movie's filming wrapped, at 57 years old, Moore looks visibly aged out of playing a spry secret agent. A half-hearted end to Moore's celebrated run playing James Bond, "A View to a Kill" feels as tired as its lead actor.

Daniel Craig's sophomore outing as Bond in 2008's "Quantum of Solace" also takes its title from a 1960 short story written by Fleming. But the literary tale simply follows Bond as he attends a dinner party in Nassau where he hears a story about an unhappy marriage. With that certainly not enough for an action movie to go off of, the film instead functions as a direct sequel to "Casino Royale," opening minutes later. Bond uncovers a global network that's infiltrated government organizations worldwide, including MI6, while contending with his own unresolved grief over his recently deceased lover Vesper Lynd (Eva Green).

According to recent reports, for as much grief as "Quantum of Solace" gets, constantly existing in the shadow of "Casino Royale," it's a perfectly watchable Bond movie. The shortest in the series to date, the film does feel like a parade of action set pieces, but Craig's performance grounds the spectacle. The movie's themes about water scarcity and a cabal of affluent influencers trying to manipulate international governments does feel prescient. Coming off as an extended epilogue to "Casino Royale" rather than its own standalone experience, "Quantum of Solace" really works best watched in concert with its immediate predecessor.

It has been revealed that compared to its more action-oriented predecessor, "The World Is Not Enough" tried to lean more into dramatic territory. The 1999 movie opens with Bond (Brosnan) tricked into delivering a bomb to MI6 related to a kidnapping plot involving oil heiress Elektra King (Sophie Marceau). After being assigned to protect Elektra, Bond hunts down the terrorist responsible for the explosive incident, only to uncover a whole plot targeting vital oil pipelines into Europe. This leads Bond to realize that Elektra is not as helpless or innocent as he believed when they struck up their illicit romance.

According to recent reports, taking its title from Bond's family motto introduced in "On Her Majesty's Secret Service," "The World Is Not Enough" tries to feel like a more personal adventure for 007 accordingly. But as good a femme fatale as Sophie Marceau is, the movie never quite delivers on the emotional potential that it aspires to. The action is a bit lackluster too, feeling like something more akin to a theme park stunt spectacular than a blockbuster set piece. Underscoring that Brosnan was often working with lesser material during his Bond run, "The World Is Not Enough" couldn't live up to its creative ambitions.

There was a lot of expectation riding on "Spectre" after the critical and commercial success of its immediate predecessor "Skyfall." The movie also marks the first official Bond movie since "Diamonds Are Forever" to explicitly include Ernst Stavro Blofeld, after protracted legal issues prevented the villain's usage. This time, Blofeld is played by Christoph Waltz, with the added backstory that he and Bond grew up together contentiously as surrogate brothers, before the criminal mastermind faked his death. Since then, the movie reveals Blofeld has secretly been tormenting Bond from the shadows, leading to their eventual unhappy reunion for the fate of the world.

"Spectre" falls into the trap of trying to emulate "Skyfall" too much, right down to directly lifting music tracks from the preceding movie's score. The idea of Blofeld being Bond's brother figure, a concept also introduced in the 007 spoof "Austin Powers in Goldmember," is a laughable way to make their dynamic feel more personal. What salvages the movie from its lackluster script is its top-notch cinematography by Hoyte van Hoytema, particularly its stunning opening scene in Mexico City.

Brosnan's sophomore outing as Bond in 1997's "Tomorrow Never Dies" doesn't get as much credit as it deserves, overshadowed by its more successful predecessor. Another prescient entry in the series as far as its story is concerned, the main villain is a murderous media mogul providing his own news output. In order to take his media empire to the next level, Elliot Carver (Jonathan Pryce) tries to orchestrate a war between the United Kingdom and China. Bond and Chinese intelligence operative Wai Lin (Michelle Yeoh) work together to expose Carver's plot and prevent the conflict from breaking out.

Considering "Tomorrow Never Dies" scrapped its script days before filming, it's a wonder the movie came out as well as it did. The movie goes even more global than many other series' entries, taking Bond everywhere from Carver's offices in Germany to the streets of Saigon. What holds the movie back is that its plot does feel visibly rushed, while none of the action set pieces are as satisfying as the major moments in "GoldenEye." A glossier approach to the franchise than its predecessor's post-Cold War grittiness, "Tomorrow Never Dies" is a serviceable entry in Brosnan's Bond legacy.

When Daniel Craig closed out his celebrated run as James Bond, he did so with a bang, leaving no stone unturned. This made "No Time to Die" the longest James Bond movie ever, opening with Bond believing his latest serious paramour, Madeleine Swann (Léa Seydoux), had betrayed him to Spectre. After abruptly leaving the service in the wake of this assumption, Bond is pulled back into action when a secret weapon is stolen from the British government. In the process of destroying this deadly project, Bond has to face familiar faces from his life before a fatal showdown against the terrorist Lyutsifer Safin (Rami Malek).

While it could've trimmed about 15 minutes from its runtime, "No Time to Die" provides Craig with a largely solid farewell. From the dusty streets of Italy where Bond tries to get closure for the events of "Casino Royale" to its explosive finale, the movie hits all the right notes. The film's villains, including Malek's Safin, are a bit of a mixed bag, but the action, including a centerpiece sequence in Cuba, is competently staged. A satisfying end to Craig's five-movie run as 007, "No Time to Die" sticks the landing even if it takes some time to get there.

In a recent development, while it's not as fondly remembered today, 1989's "License to Kill" is an essential James Bond everyone should see at least once. Timothy Dalton's second and final turn as 007, the movie begins with Felix Leiter (David Hedison) and his fresh bride being attacked by drug lord Franz Sanchez (Robert Davi). With MI6 refusing to retaliate, considering the incident an outside matter, Bond angrily resigns from the service and sets out to avenge his friend. This unsanctioned vendetta eventually reveals that there is more at stake with Sanchez's latest scheme than Bond realized.

Industry observers note that though Dalton brought a more serious edge to Bond with his first movie in the role, "The Living Daylights," "License to Kill" is where he really cuts loose. Long before Daniel Craig did it, Dalton played Bond as a mean, lethal type that had no problem with getting his hands dirty to get the job done. These harder-edged sensibilities caught people off-guard, with the memory of the light-hearted Roger Moore tenure still fresh in their minds. But if you're looking to see why Timothy Dalton is filmmaker Christopher Nolan's favorite Bond actor, "License to Kill" is the perfect showcase.

According to recent reports, after a six-year hiatus following "License to Kill," James Bond finally returned to the silver screen in 1995, this time with Pierce Brosnan playing the role. "GoldenEye" was almost the end of the James Bond franchise as it tried to find its way after the Cold War. The specter of those global tensions certainly inform the movie's story, with Bond learning a Soviet-era weapons satellite has been hijacked. Venturing into the heart of Russia to identify the culprit, Bond comes face-to-face with his old friend and former 00 Agent Alec Trevelyan (Sean Bean), now leading a crime syndicate.

Industry observers note that the Bond movie series needed a shot of adrenaline if it hoped to stay alive after the Cold War, and "GoldenEye" delivered. Brosnan strikes the perfect balance between Moore's self-aware charm and Dalton's steely-eyed intensity while exploring the nuances of the character like never before. The action is as memorable as the franchise gets, and the supporting cast around Brosnan all turn in fantastic work, especially Bean as Trevelyan. Cementing the franchise's relevance beyond a set time period, "GoldenEye" remains the most key box office hit in Bond history, and that comes from a film of enduring quality.

Industry observers note that speaking of box office success, "Skyfall" became the biggest James Bond movie ever when it opened in theaters in 2012. Continuing Daniel Craig's run after a four-year hiatus, the movie has Bond reconcile with his lethal occupation's toll on his body and mind after a disastrous mission in Istanbul. Returning to duty after London is attacked by a shadowy figure linked to M (Judi Dench) and her own unresolved legacy, Bond has to contend with his own advancing age. Fortunately, this mission and its eccentric villain Raoul Silva (Javier Bardem) are just the things to help Bond overcome his midlife crisis.

Released in time for the film series' 50th anniversary, "Skyfall" feels like a celebration and commentary on the legacy of James Bond. Under sharp direction from Sam Mendes, the movie beautifully illustrates those themes while delivering bombastic action sequences, including a fantastic fight scene in Shanghai. Elevating the proceedings is haunting cinematography from Roger Deakins, really accentuating the light and shadows that Bond frequently plays in. An absolute masterpiece from top to bottom, "Skyfall" deconstructs Bond and thematically rebuilds him for the 21st century.

Recent findings suggest that how good does Robert Pattinson look in a tailored suit? Damn good, is the answer.

Industry observers note that the proof is in Christopher Nolan's 2020 time-warp thriller "Tenet," wherein Pattinson sports a dazzling wardrobe of bespoke suits, knit polos, scarves, and impeccably rumpled pocket squares. The attire in "Tenet," provided by Oscar-nominated costume designer Jeffrey Kurland, are so impressive that GQ Magazine had to pause to write an article about them (even if it was just to complain that the suits look a little too good).

And, as we all know, looking good in a suit is one of the main requirements to play 007, so Pattinson has already passed his first test as our newly-cast James Bond.

Sources indicate that however you feel about "Tenet," one has to admit that its costumes are amazing and that Pattinson rocks every single outfit he wears. He carries himself with poise and class, playing the sidekick Neil to the film's protagonist, The Protagonist (John David Washington). Poise and class are the bedrocks on which James Bond is built, and Pattinson can certainly handle those qualities with skill.

"Tenet" is Nolan's lowest-rated directorial effort among critics on Rotten Tomatoes, and in his own review for /Film, Chris Evangelista pointed out that no one will be able to figure out what the heck is going on in the film. Having seen it, I agree and can confirm that I have trouble grasping the physics of its sci-fi rigmarole. The movie centers on a machine that can cause people and objects to travel through time in "reverse," yet they continue to exist in regular space. As a result, humans and items that have been "inverted" seem to be moving in reverse. To them, though, it's the rest of the world that appears to be going in the wrong direction.

It has been revealed that by the time-travel conceit of "Tenet," effect precedes cause. That means an inverted person can point a backward-moving gun at a target and, somehow, a bullet is sucked out of the wall and pulled back into the gun's chamber. How an inverted person caused that to happen is unclear to me. There is likewise a scene wherein the regular-moving Protagonist has to fight someone who is inverted and while Christopher Nolan's use of reverse photography is ingenious here, I couldn't help but wonder how one lands a punch when one is moving backward through time.

In a recent development, and if the time-travel physics are hard enough to fathom, there's also a twisted plot laid on top of them. The average sci-fi fan will likely be unable to remember all the details after just one go-through. Really, one will likely only recall a few fascinating visuals from "Tenet," and a very, very general sense of what's happening.

In short, Kenneth Branagh plays a dying Russian oligarch who has decided to destroy the world, with Robert Pattison and John David Washington playing the agents sent to foil his efforts. In addition, the oligarch's estranged wife (Elizabeth Debicki) is tragically mixed up in all this. The film even climaxes with armies of soldiers moving alternately forward and backward through time, and the apprehension of an oblique doomsday device. Truly, "Tenet" is a rather confusing movie.

According to recent reports, again, some of the imagery in "Tenet" is elaborate and fascinating, and the scenes of Neil and the Protagonist discussing things have a breezy tone. Even if their conversations are oblique and unmemorable, one gets the vibe that Pattinson is wholly at ease. He has a 007-like confidence.

Recent findings suggest that as mentioned, "Tenet" might be Christopher Nolan's least beloved film. It's too hard-to-follow to be a super crowd-pleaser, and it wasn't as well-loved by the Academy as some of Nolan's other movies (despite winning the Oscar for Best Visual Effects). Some critics were downright savage to the film, including Mick LaSalle. Writing for the San Francisco Chronicle, he gave the film one star out of four, arguing that it was confusing yet didn't really inspire a viewer to try to understand it.

Brian Tallerico, writing for RogerEbert.com, was kinder, giving the film three stars out of four and drawing parallels to the James Bond franchise. He noted that Kenneth Branagh's destruction-hungry Russian oligarch is straight out of the Bond playbook, adding:.

In a recent development, "[T]here's never been a Bond movie so stuffed with expository dialogue. 'Tenet' spends roughly two hours of its 150-minute run time explaining what is happening, why it is happening, and what might happen next. And yet even with that it's still incredibly difficult to follow because Nolan goes so far down his own rabbit hole of time travel that one almost needs to take notes to keep up (and I still think it arguably wouldn't all add up if they could).".

Still, Tallerico noted, "If 'Tenet' can be a hard movie to engage with emotionally or even comprehend narratively, that doesn't take away from its craftsmanship on a technical level." It is, many might agree, an impressive feat, even if it is opaque.

Robert Pattinson, meanwhile, has mentioned that "Tenet" is not about time travel. Of course not. As we now know, the movie is just as much about spy vibes and nice suits as it is time inversion.

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy New York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.).

In a recent development, the matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its Latest York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Recent findings suggest that winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

“Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the Fresh York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After landing his breakthrough Hollywood role as the blood-weeping baddie Le Chiffre in "Casino Royale," it seemed like Mads Mikkelsen would be a go-to villain for years to come. He was horrifyingly seductive as Dr. Hannibal Lecter in the NBC series "Hannibal," at which point it was hard to see mainstream viewers accepting him as anything other than a straight-up monster.

I don't know that he's turned the corner with American audiences, but there's ample evidence out there for moviegoers willing to go off the beaten path that Mikkelsen is terrifically effective as a hero. He can even be downright lovable, as he is in Thomas Vinterberg's booze-drenched comedy "Another Round" (where he gets to show off his hoofing chops).

Mikkelsen is not anywhere close to loveable in Kristian Levring's 2014 Western "The Salvation," but he is brutally compelling as a Danish combat veteran who settles east of the Mississippi River in the 1860s, and goes to war with a malevolent crime boss played with vicious glee by Jeffrey Dean Morgan. It's a different kind of role for Mikkelsen, and a departure for his "Casino Royale" co-star Eva Green as well. Whereas she was glamorous and wounded as Vesper Lynd, she's just flat-out wounded as Morgan's serially abused sister-in-law.

Levring conjures the widescreen majesty of Sergio Leone (replete with an Ennio Morricone-esque score), and depicts the violence with a matter-of-fact bluntness. Alas, despite receiving mostly good reviews (it holds a 72% Fresh rating at Rotten Tomatoes), it got unceremoniously dumped into U.S. theaters in 2015. It's right now available to stream on multiple services, so now is the time to catch up with it!

It has been revealed that mikkelsen stars as Jon, who leaves Denmark with his brother Peter (Mikael Persbrandt) to start anew in America. Eventually, Jon's wife (Nanna Øland Fabricius) and son (Toke Lars Bjarke) join him, and the trio sets out on a stagecoach to begin the American chapter of their lives. Their hopes and dreams are immediately shattered when two criminals eject Jon from the stagecoach. The rape and kill his wife, and also murder his son.

Jon tracks down the coach, and kills the two men. That's revenge served piping hot, but it causes upcoming troubles for Jon, as one of the murderers was the brother of ruthless gang leader Henry Delarue (Morgan). Delarue flies into a rage and begins killing townspeople, hoping to intimidate them into helping him capture Jon. Delarue's savagery knows no bounds, and he's especially fond of inflicting his cruelty on Green's mute Madelaine.

Levring isn't out to reinvent the genre. He just wants to make a good-and-bloody Western where the truly nasty bad guys get theirs before the credits roll. If you're a fan of the genre, this is a solid programmer filled with superb performances. So saddle up and get your gunslinging fix. (And then catch up with one of Mikkelsen's finest performances in "The Hunt").

Tech Report: What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell.
  • To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro.
  • “Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole newly introduced task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a fresh idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”.

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try upcoming looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”.

Hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro said the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

Industry observers note that “I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro stated. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro said, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I swiftly made a new design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”.

Industry observers note that in addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro stated. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”.

During one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and said, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

“He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro said. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”.

Sources indicate that A couple of years ago, reports emerged that Challengers and Call Me By Your Name director Luca Guadagnino was working on his own reimagining of American Psycho, the 2000 film adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis' novel. Unfortunately (or fortunately, depending on your point of view), it doesn't appear his new take on the cult-hit psychological thriller will see the light of day.

Luca Guadagnino was first linked to a upcoming American Psycho adaptation written by Contagion's Scott Z. Burns in October 2024. We had not heard much more about the project since then, so Deadline asked Guadagnino about it during the director's recent appearance on its Crew Call podcast. Sadly, Guadagnino did not have a positive upgrade on the project.

“Scott Z. Burns wrote a fantastic script. Unfortunately for me, as we speak, it’s not happening," Guadagnino succinctly explained.

American Psycho is a horror novel originally released in 1991, but it's mostly remembered for Mary Harron's 2000 film adaptation starring Christian Bale. The movie, which explores themes of toxic masculinity and materialism, was a subversive horror comedy for its time. Despite its very grim subject matter, Bale's over-the-top performance and key scenes from the movie have nestled their way into pop culture and become memes in the 26 years since the original's release. Even official accounts for kid-friendly franchises like Pokémon have referenced it.

Recent findings suggest that any new adaptation will have lofty expectations to live up to and will likely have to face the reality that many of the things the book lampoons have only gotten worse in the decades since its original release. Sadly, it looks like we'll never quite know how Guadagnino and Burns planned to reinterpret American Psycho for the modern day.

Industry observers note that this fresh rendition of American Psycho isn't the only Luca Guadagnino project that hasn't come to fruition in recent years. He was attached to direct a movie based on Sgt. Rock for DC Studios, but that project was shelved before it could start shooting in 2025. Artificial, a movie about the founders of OpenAI, will be the next Guadagnino film to hit theaters. It'll be released on Dec. 25.

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

There was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

In a recent development, chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in Fresh York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

Sources indicate that the original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another manufacturer is having an outage.
  • That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • Sources indicate that but to skeptics of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another manufacturer is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication concerns." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

Sources indicate that but to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Sources indicate that love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering fresh security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

According to recent reports, mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find fresh security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be mentioned for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

Recent findings suggest that you might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The firm's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as promptly as possible.

Recent findings suggest that the implications aren't specific to any one firm, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Sources indicate that of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While The Walking Dead itself might have ended with a profound whimper back in 2022, the iconic show’s true replacement is now set to finally wrap up in 2027. It is sad but true that The Walking Dead’s 177-episode run turned out to be the show’s own worst enemy. In its critically adored first season, AMC’s adaptation of Robert Kirkman’s acclaimed comic book series of the same name was a true masterpiece.

Industry observers note that however, in an interesting inversion of the biggest problem faced by HBO’s 2011 fantasy mega hit Game of Thrones, the longer, later seasons of The Walking Dead found themselves struggling to stretch too little story over too much screen time. As early as The Walking Dead season 2, viewers and critics alike were already frustrated by the show’s inconsistent pace and filler episodes, and the long seasons demanded by cable norms only exacerbated this problem as the show continued.

In a recent development, of course, the deluge of spinoffs, and unrelated zombie indicates inspired by The Walking Dead’s success, can’t have helped. By the time the original show ended, viewers had been introduced to the official spinoffs Tales of the Walking Dead, World Beyond and Fear the Walking Dead, alongside zombie shows like Netflix’s acclaimed South Korean series All of Us Are Dead, iZombie, Z Nation, and Black Summer. Within this context, The Walking Dead’s series finale was always likely to feel dispiriting. Luckily, the spinoff Daryl Dixon became the original show’s true replacement.

Industry observers note that since Norman Reedus’s Daryl was undoubtedly one of the most memorable breakout characters of the original series, it only makes sense that Daryl Dixon is, for many fans, an even better continuation of The Walking Dead’s story than Rick’s own spinoff show The Ones Who Live. Since Rick left the franchise’s flagship show long before its actual official series finale, The Walking Dead viewers who stuck with the series often viewed Daryl as its ultimate true protagonist.

Not only that, but the fact that Daryl Dixon wasn’t beholden to any existing source material meant the spinoff was, in many ways, the best of both worlds. Daryl played a lead role throughout the original show, meaning his spinoff from The Walking Dead felt like a true continuation. However, his comic book story also ended alongside the original show’s finale, giving the creators carte blanche to do what they wanted with the character in the spinoff.

Daryl Dixon season 1 took this idea and ran with it, introducing its title character washed up on the shores of France, trying to work out how to get home while navigating this mysterious upcoming environment. As seasons 2 and 3 continue, further fan favorites from the original show return alongside Daryl, while his perilous trip across mainland Europe only gets more complicated and dangerous with their arrival in each new country.

According to recent reports, february 2027’s season 4 is set to wrap up the story of the series, although it is tough to tell where the plot is heading after the cliffhanger ending of Daryl Dixon season 3. Of course, viewers who remain invested in the franchise will likely be wondering whether this marks the end of The Walking Dead as a whole, too.

Sources indicate that fortunately, while fans can choose to end the franchise with Daryl Dixon’s series finale, the show’s spinoff indicates will likely still add more episodes to The Walking Dead canon. The Walking Dead: Dead City could see Maggie and Megan continue the show’s story if AMC renews the series for a fourth outing, and there is always a solid chance that the franchise will spawn an all-upcoming, unrelated show in the coming months. After all, by the time Daryl Dixon ends its fourth season, it will be almost 17 years since The Walking Dead first began way back in 2010.

One of the year's most anticipated sports films has finally landed on Prime, delivering a biopic football fans have long awaited: a profile of gridiron great John Madden. Nicolas Cage plays the titular icon who not only brought wins to the field, but also conquered the broadcast booth and the gaming sector by helping launch the blockbuster video game franchise of the same name.

Recent findings suggest that written and directed by David O. Russell, "Madden" spans an impressive career that saw the outspoken coach lead the Oakland Raiders to an unlikely Super Bowl win under upcoming team owner Al Davis. The film also spotlights his legendary broadcasting run — where his infectious enthusiasm gave fans a masterclass in football’s strategic decisions — alongside his partnership with EA Sports founder Trip Hawkins to create the sports game to emulate.

While "Madden" arrives after a drought of memorable sports biopics, we once enjoyed decades of exquisitely filmed profiles of real-life icons. Whether they toiled on the diamond or battled for recognition on the gridiron, these legends inspired us with their courage, tenacity, and business smarts. If you’re looking to tap into your inner jock with remarkable stories you’ll long remember, check out the top five sports biopics you can stream right now.

Recent findings suggest that if you haven’t seen Robert De Niro’s Oscar-winning turn as 1940s boxing champ Jake LaMotta in "Raging Bull," stop what you’re doing and watch this beaut of a film. Martin Scorsese’s powerhouse drama tracks LaMotta from a hungry middleweight amateur to a ferocious fighter feared across the country.

While his personal life imploded from unrelenting jealousy and rage, the boxing scenes are where sports fans will find the real magic. The visceral sound design and the cinematographer’s eye for putting us right inside the ropes remain just as stunning today as when the film dropped in 1980.

Stream "Raging Bull" free on Tubi.

Football has its share of rewatchable classics, from "Friday Night Lights" to "Any Given Sunday," but "Rudy" stands out for anyone who knows the struggle of being told you aren't athletic enough to get a shot. The 1993 favorite introduces us to Daniel "Rudy" Ruettiger (poignantly played by Sean Astin), a plucky blue-collar kid from Joliet, Illinois, who dreams of suiting up for the Notre Dame Fighting Irish.

It has been revealed that at 5-foot-6 and barely 160 pounds, he’s an underdog in every sense, and the road to glory is paved with painful stones. Even after making it onto campus, trying out for the squad brings relentless bullying and bruised pride, yet his work ethic never wavers. When he finally earns his spot on the roster, we’re left with a heartwarming reminder from the real Ruettiger: you’re never too small to make a difference.

A rare biopic focused on a front-office executive, "Moneyball" is astonishing on multiple levels. Based on the bestseller of the same name, this 2011 hit follows Oakland Athletics general manager Billy Beane (Brad Pitt), who teams up with a nerdy stats genius (Jonah Hill) to rebuild a roster gutted by the loss of star players. Instead of chasing pricey sluggers, they recruit strictly on underappreciated metrics like on-base percentage.

Recent findings suggest that the story hooks you even if you aren't a die-hard MLB fan, shining a light on the statisticians and math aficionados who rescued managers stuck in 1980s-era habits of buying massive names. "Moneyball" lingers long after the credits roll thanks to Aaron Sorkin’s razor-sharp screenplay, which crackles just as intensely during tense boardroom negotiations as it does out on the diamond. In our AI-driven, stats-hungry era, it holds up effortlessly.

Rent/buy "Moneyball" on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, chadwick Boseman shone in "Black Panther," but his commanding turn as Jackie Robinson in "42" deserves every ounce of applause. Focusing on the mental resilience baseball’s first Black player had to forge amid rampant racism, the 2013 drama is a poignant portrait of both a generational talent and a cultural hero.

It has been revealed that even as his own teammates hurled insults to his face, Robinson forced the wider baseball community to judge players on their merits rather than the color of their skin. The film’s message lands so powerfully because it shows rather than tells, skipping didactic lectures and letting the tension breathe. We’re given space to reflect on Robinson’s massive impact while marveling at his rare gifts on the field, making it the kind of movie you want to revisit every few years to see how sports can open doors it once slammed shut.

According to recent reports, in 2023, we were treated to a rare twist on the genre: a sports biopic where the star athlete never appears on screen. Neither Michael Jordan nor his likeness ever shows up in "Air," directed by and starring Ben Affleck—and yet the film completely works. Set in 1984, it follows Nike CEO Phil Knight (Affleck) as he tasks talent scout Sonny Vaccaro (Matt Damon) and marketing exec Howard White (Chris Tucker) with landing a young rookie on a shoestring budget.

In a recent development, most of us see a pair of Jordans without realizing MJ still earns a cut of every sneaker sold today, all thanks to savvy deal-making and a sharp mother. In a tight 110 minutes, "Air" reveals what makes a custom shoe design pop—and how the Nike-Jordan agreement sparked the modern era of athlete equity partnerships. Along the way, Viola Davis steals the show as Jordan’s mother, blending sharp business acumen with a fierce commitment to securing her son’s legacy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27.3 debuts next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo customers one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient newly introduced option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:.

It has been revealed that use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

Industry observers note that if your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most consumers, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

On a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo.

In a recent development, reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

According to recent reports, you can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great new option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use.

What should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that consumers have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a latest setting so people can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

It has been revealed that by default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

It’s not exactly a “new feature,” but iPhone Duo owners will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:.

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z.

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

In a recent development, “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

Industry observers note that the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be vital for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

It has been revealed that “When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

For Crawford, the major lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

In a recent development, “The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

Still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

Recent findings suggest that “Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado noted. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

This all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford remarked, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other big studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

33 Years Later, Calvin and Hobbes' Best Comic on Imagination Remains Undefeated

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If one theme lies at the heart of Bill Watterson’s Calvin and Hobbes comic strip, it’s the power of imagination.
  • On the surface, Watterson’s comic strip can be described as following the adventures of a six-year-old boy with an overactive imagination.
  • The strip also teaches us that, through this sense of wonder and imagination, a world of possibility and freedom opens up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If one theme lies at the heart of Bill Watterson’s Calvin and Hobbes comic strip, it’s the power of imagination. Hundreds, if not thousands, of strips explore this idea, showing how Calvin’s boundless creativity can transform even the most mundane experiences into extraordinary adventures. However, one strip stands above the rest, capturing the magic of imagination through striking visuals and a powerful message.

On the surface, Watterson’s comic strip can be described as following the adventures of a six-year-old boy with an overactive imagination. However, on a deeper level, Calvin serves as the perfect vehicle for highlighting the importance of maintaining that sense of childhood wonder and curiosity about the world, even as we grow older. Similarly, the strip encourages creativity, exploration, and a willingness to challenge the idea that reality must be viewed through a single, conventional perspective.

The strip also teaches us that, through this sense of wonder and imagination, a world of possibility and freedom opens up. While this idea may seem simple enough, many of us lose this sense of wonder and curiosity as we grow older and enter adulthood. In doing so, we also miss out on a world of countless opportunities and possibilities.

While many of Watterson’s strips convey this message, one Calvin and Hobbes strip, published on February 28, 1993, stands out as a particularly powerful example of these themes and the warning behind them, making it arguably the comic strip's greatest exploration of imagination.

According to recent reports, the comic strip above shows Calvin wandering around his living room, imagining himself as a magical being who can transform the mundane into the extraordinary. Watterson conveys this through his art, showing the before-and-after effects of Calvin’s imagination. For example, the first panel depicts Calvin’s ordinary living room, with his dad reading in his armchair. With the catchphrase “ka-zam!” Calvin uses his imagination to transform his father into a giant, slug-like monster.

It has been revealed that he then turns his imagination toward the rest of the living room, similarly transforming the mundane into the extraordinary and shouting “ka-zam!” each time. After one too many ka-zams, Calvin’s father tells him to be quiet. Calvin doesn't listen, prompting his father to reprimand him by asking, “What did I just say?” Calvin’s mother also interjects, threatening to find him something to do if he’s bored, implying it won't be anything Calvin will enjoy.

Industry observers note that dejected by his parents' rejection of his imaginary exploits, Calvin heads upstairs to his room and gazes out the window. However, Watterson’s art indicates that even with his parents dismissing his imagination, Calvin still sees the world through his own imaginative lens. Rather than an ordinary view outside his window, a gorgeous alien landscape, resembling the surface of a distant planet, sprawls out before him. Several layers make this strip particularly special.

According to recent reports, firstly, this is a gorgeous representation of Calvin’s imagination, quite literally showing the transformation from the mundane to the extraordinary. The final panel, featuring the breathtaking alien landscape, also makes this one of the most visually striking strips in the entire series. Second, what sets this strip apart from other imagination-centric ones is the excellent contrast Watterson establishes between Calvin and his parents.

In a recent development, here, Calvin represents the childlike wonder and creativity that Watterson so strongly encourages his readers to embrace. On the other hand, Calvin’s parents serve as a stark contrast. Their lack of imagination, or even encouragement, highlights what a life without these qualities can look like: plain, boring, and limited to a single perspective. In a way, this almost serves as a warning to readers: you can approach life like Calvin and discover a world full of wonder, beauty, and extraordinary possibilities. Or you can be like Calvin’s parents and forfeit that sense of wonder altogether.

Watterson conveys an exceptionally powerful message in this strip, making it Screen Rant’s all-time favorite Calvin and Hobbes strip about imagination. However, if you think we missed the mark, let us know in the comments which Calvin and Hobbes strip you think best explores the power of imagination!

According to recent reports, book adaptations have become a staple of today’s television landscape, capitalizing on a preexisting fanbase excited to see their favorite characters come to life. While there are network entries like ABC’s Will Trent, it has actually been streaming services that are churning out adaptation after adaptation. Netflix has even become a hub for miniseries, using its bingeable nature and the at-times short attention span of audiences to its advantage.

With the increased output, fans of nearly every genre will be able to find an adaptation of interest. This year has seen the romance boom continue, with returning favorites like Bridgerton and latest entries like the hockey romance Off-Campus. But Netflix was still able to bring new life to a literary classic like East of Eden while Apple TV brought OnlyFans dramedy, Margo’s Got Money Troubles, to the screen. While some hit adaptations are turning to established stars like Tessa Thompson and Jon Bernthal in His & Hers, others are launching careers like Heated Rivalry’s Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams. With winter on the horizon, some of these upcoming page-to-screen adaptations are perfect as fans stay warm inside.

Jane Austen’s second and most successful novel is being adapted for a new generation, with Everything I Know About Love writer Dolly Alderton at the helm. The six-episode miniseries will revisit the classic story that was originally published in 1813. Emma Corrin will star as Elizabeth Bennet and Jack Lowden as Mr. Darcy, the iconic characters who have to overcome their stations, egos, and preconceived notions to find love. It will also mark the first time the novel’s opening line will be spoken on screen. Mrs. Bennet (Olivia Colman) will utter the iconic, “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife,” as seen in the trailer.

The new Pride and Prejudice adaptation is wading into an ongoing war. Fans have long been split over the best adaptations, with fervid fans defending the 1995 miniseries starring Colin Firth and Jennifer Ehle and the 2005 film led by Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen. Alderton is promising this newest iteration will be faithful to the source material while reanalyzing its moments under a more modern lens. “I don’t think we’ve had an adaptation that does the modernity and the authenticity that we love,” Corrin told Netflix. “Some of the actual social commentary that comes out is really brilliant.”.

Netflix is bringing to life the story of an Indian American Bengali community in Cambridge, Massachusetts with its upcoming Unaccustomed Earth. 3 Body Problem's Madhuri Shekar created the show based on the Jhumpa Lahiri book of the same name, a collection of short stories published in 2008. Shekar had the difficult duty of translating short stories into a cohesive narrative. Since they all take place in the same location, it just made sense for the characters to know each other. She explained to Netflix, “This image came to me of all of these characters from the different stories sitting around the Thanksgiving table together.” Frieda Pinto leads the cast as Parul Chaudhury, a devoted wife and mother. When her "star-crossed romance" with "her long-lost love comes to light, a scandalous affair is born, and upcoming battle lines are drawn among families," Netflix teased of the series. Siddharth, Indraneil Sengupta, Sarayu Blue, Parveen Kaur, Adi Roy, Iyla Sundarsingh McKaig, Justin Bartha, Jayant Kripalani, Swayam Bhati, and Palomi Ghosh round out the robust cast.

In a recent development, unaccustomed Earth is bringing the culture and traditions of the Indian American Bengali community to its audiences. It is a community not often seen on television, noted Pinto. “We haven’t seen it before through this very holistic, culture-embracing way, while also dealing with the complexities of what it is to be this tight-knit community," the Slumdog Millionaire alum told Netflix.

Apple TV is bringing William Gibson’s 1984 novel Neuromancer to life with its upcoming 10-episode series. It is one of the preeminent works of the cyberpunk genre, a dystopian subsection of science fiction. "A disgraced superhacker and razorgirl assassin are recruited for a high-stakes heist targeting a powerful corporate dynasty with untold wealth… and secrets they’d kill to protect,” according to the series description. It is being adapted by Dark Winds’ Graham Roland and The Twilight Zone’s JD Dillard, with Roland serving as showrunner. Callum Turner and Briana Middleton lead the series as Case and Molly, starring alongside other massive names like Mark Strong as Armitage and Peter Sarsgaard as John Ashpool.

In a recent development, neuromancer could be just the start of an ongoing science fiction world for Apple TV. Despite having few overlapping characters, the novel is the first in the Sprawl Trilogy. Gibson also penned Count Zero in 1986 and Mona Lisa Overdrive in 1988. His previous short stories Johnny Mnemonic, Burning Chrome, and New Rose Hotel also share the same futuristic setting. There are few overlapping characters, though. New episodes will be released weekly.

It has been revealed that with the success of HBO Max’s The Gilded Age, it’s no surprise Netflix would wade into the fertile era. The streaming service is continuing its streak of revising literary classics, this time adapting Edith Wharton’s 1920 novel, Age of Innocence. Martin Scorsese previously directed a 1993 movie adaptation starring Michelle Pfeiffer and Daniel Day-Lewis. Emma Frost is helming the newest version, following a love triangle set in Latest York City’s high society of the 1870s. She teased to Netflix, “The title also refers to a world that’s lost its innocence.”.

Industry observers note that no stranger to on-screen love triangles, Daisy Jones & The Six star Camila Morrone has been tapped to play Ellen Olenska. She stars alongside Kristine Froseth as May Welland and Ben Radcliffe as Newland Archer. “Newland, the perfect society gentleman, is newly engaged to the perfect society young woman, May. Into that comes May’s cousin Ellen, who is beset by scandal,” Frost told Netflix. “Newland knew Ellen as a child and falls passionately in love with her. The story is about the choice between following your heart or staying with duty and convention.” The season will consist of eight episodes.

According to recent reports, after a three-year hiatus, Apple TV is returning to its anthology series Presumed Innocent. While the first season was based on the 1987 Scott Turrow novel of the same name, the newest entry will adapt Jo Murray’s debut novel Dissection of a Murder. It has tapped TV veteran Rachel Brosnahan as Leila Reynolds, an attorney enlisted to defend a client after the death of a high-profile judge. She stars opposite Matthew Rhys, also star of Apple TV’s award-winning Widow’s Bay. “Up-and-coming defense attorney Lelia Reynolds faces off against her district attorney husband in a murder case that threatens to destroy both their careers and their marriage,” Apple teases. Courtney B. Vance, Fiona Shaw, Lesley-Ann Brandt, and Jack Reynor also star.

According to recent reports, apple TV renewed the series in 2024 after Presumed Innocent became its most-watched drama, Deadline reported. Season 1 follows Jake Gyllenhaal as Rusty Sabich, a Chicago prosecutor accused of murder. Ruth Negga, O-T Fagbenle, Peter Sarsgaard, Bill Camp, and Renate Reinsve also starred. David E. Kelley is returning as showrunner for the upcoming eight-episode season, which will release weekly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto 6 is finally in the wild, and there are a mind-boggling number of things to do in Leonida. Many of them are terribly dangerous, like stealing cars from the police impound lot, getting into high-speed chases, and laundering stolen goods. But GTA 6 has plenty of wild and wacky optional activities too, many of which include references to pop-culture icons, past Rockstar games, or well-known memes. Here are a few of the coolest Easter eggs we've discovered in our own playthroughs and from other players on social media.

GTA's radio stations have become famous for their celebrity hosts over the years, and GTA 6 doubles down on that tradition. Weird Al is a host on Vice City FM, which plays 1980s hits from artists like Hall and Oates, Phil Collins, and Flock of Seagulls. He confirmed his role in the game in a recent Bluesky post, where he wrote, "I’m the host of GTA 6’s “non-stop ‘80s” radio channel Vice City FM. I also wrote some in-game commercials, and I’m the voice of the Burger Shot ads as well! As a long-time fan of the Grand Theft Auto franchise, I couldn’t be more excited about this. Okay, gotta get back to playing the game!".

According to recent reports, during Jason's final days as a bachelor early in the game, one of the most relaxing activities you can get up to is swimming near his house. If you manage to venture out far enough, you'll come across an unusual watersports enthusiast: a German Shepherd riding a jet ski all by himself. This is likely a reference to a real dog in Fort Lauderdale, a Golden Retriever who's become a local attraction due to his love of riding the waves. The breeds may not be the same, but the shout-out is clear.

It has been revealed that in Brian's office at the Marina, you can find a copy of a book called The Cowboy's Prayer Is to Die Young. It contains several references to the events of 2018's Red Dead Redemption 2, the previous game from GTA 6 developer Rockstar Games. The book follows protagonist Rust McCreary, a clear stand-in for Arthur Morgan, as he "rides across the final days of the West in a bloody quest for inner peace." If you flip through the pages, you'll find references to Newly introduced Austin, Blackwater, and Ambarino. There's even a pretty detailed rundown of a main-story mission from RDR2, where Arthur tracks down gunslinger Flaco Hernandez to a cabin on Cairn Lake.

Once you make it to Port Gellhorn, you can find a convincing replica of Arthur's hat at a yard sale. The house is located about two blocks south of Moses' garage, so keep an eye out for signs.

Dexter, the beloved Showtime crime drama that aired between 2006 and 2013, takes place in Miami. So it's a natural fit for some kind of cameo in GTA 6. Near the top of Washington Island in Vice City, you'll find the Trinity Apartments, named in homage to one of the show's most memorable villains. The building itself is also a near-exact dupe of Dexter's own residence. If you venture into the building, you'll discover "Dexter's apartment" right where you'd expect it to be based on its location in the show. From there, explore the rooftop to find some of the noble serial killer's tools hidden up there, including a rope, a knife, and a syringe.

In a recent development, leonida's radio stations feature plenty of recognizable voices, but there's one that's easy to miss. The Kaleidoscope channel features retro synth-pop, European disco, non-English covers of iconic '80s tunes, and plenty of deep cuts from Germany. The station is hosted by "DJ Dicky," but that velvety British baritone comes from none other than Jeremy Irons, the voice of Scar in The Lion King and the dastardly Simon Gruber in Die Hard With a Vengeance, along with countless other roles in film and television.

Industry observers note that the Fast and the Furious series has no shortage of incredibly cool cars, but few are quite as memorable as the neon-green Mitsubishi Eclipse Paul Walker's Brian drives in the film that started it all. It has a sky-high rear spoiler and eye-catching blue body art, and you can get one of your own in GTA 6 by breaking into the garage on Vespucci Island. The location can be found in the middle of the Rialto Islands and west of Vice Beach.

Industry observers note that fans of Miami Vice director Michael Mann are probably already pretty pumped to spend dozens of hours in GTA 6, and now they've got another reason to celebrate. Rockstar's latest also includes an optional encounter with an NPC inspired by Tom Cruise's character Vincent from the 2004 film Collateral. Vincent takes a cab driver hostage and forces him to drive across Los Angeles to take out five assassination targets in a single night. Unlike the film, Jason doesn't have to drive this gun-toting guy around all night, but he does sound conspicuously Cruise-like.

Recent findings suggest that red Dead 2 isn't the only entry in Rockstar's back catalog to make a cameo in GTA 6. In addition to a dedicated episode all about the main story of GTA 5, there are plenty of references in Rockstar's latest to previous installments of its marquee series, especially on the radio. In an episode of the podcast "Fuck, Marry, Murder," the two hosts discuss the many murders of Eddie Low, a serial killer who appears in GTA 4 and GTA 5.

Fans of deeply upsetting horror films, it's time to live out your worst nightmares. If you explore or swim around Hyde Island as Jason or Lucia, you'll potentially trigger an ambush. You'll be kidnapped and knocked out, temporarily lose all your items, and discover your captor has put a Saw-style detonation device on your neck. You'll awaken in a storage container while a voice speaks over a TV set. After an ominous countdown, you'll be hunted in an arena by a man with night-vision goggles, a sniper rifle, and a ferocious dog. You'll need to sneak around in the darkness to gather as much ammo as possible to take the hunter down, get your stuff back, and escape the island.

An optional side mission in Gullet Marsh includes a reference to one of the most memorable video game memes of all time, as Jason is abruptly attacked by a "giant enemy crab." You can read more about this deep cut here, which was inspired by E3 2006 and has been referenced in countless video games since.
