The 10 Best Documentaries in Cinema History, Ranked

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Documentaries can sometimes involve a lack of filmmaking craft, but ignoring all movies that qualify as documentaries would be foolish.
  • Some of the best documentaries of all time are also up there among the best films of all time.
  • Recent findings suggest that about as artistic and mesmerizing as sports footage can get, Tokyo Olympiad is a masterful and distinctive presentation of the 1964 Tokyo Summer Olympics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Documentaries can sometimes involve a lack of filmmaking craft, but ignoring all movies that qualify as documentaries would be foolish. Yes, plenty of them bleed together, and there is a certain style that many have which gets tedious after a while (like that generic Netflix style, when it feels like they're all scored, written, and edited by the same couple of people), yet the ones that go a little further or take more risks are special.

Some of the best documentaries of all time are also up there among the best films of all time. Like, the following documentaries are especially great, being among the best in cinema history, and with just as much to offer as any number of great non-documentary movies, if you're looking at how they're structured, directed, edited, and scored. Taken together, they all help show how versatile the documentary genre can genuinely be; far more so than some give it credit for.

Recent findings suggest that about as artistic and mesmerizing as sports footage can get, Tokyo Olympiad is a masterful and distinctive presentation of the 1964 Tokyo Summer Olympics. It’s long, with a runtime of nearly three hours, but that length allows it to cover a lot, including the opening and closing ceremonies, then all of the many, many sports in between, with each event selected captured in unbelievable detail.

And sure, watching any sport if you're into the sport is cool, but done in this way elevates things. Tokyo Olympiad, rest assured, is far more than just a clip show, as all the camera angles are far more interesting than what you'd see on a TV broadcast, and the editing plays a huge role in enhancing everything, with the use of slow-motion being particularly notable. Even for those who don't like watching sports, Tokyo Olympiad is surprisingly riveting, not to mention a great historical document of an Olympic ceremony held over six decades ago now.

According to recent reports, though The Act of Killing isn't a horror movie by any means, it feels more brutal and terrifying than most full-on horror movies actually manage to be. Part of that comes down to it covering an incredibly difficult subject, and then further, it does that in a unique and stomach-churning way, focusing on the Indonesian mass killings of 1965-1966 which saw somewhere between 500,000 and 1 million people being killed (mostly people associated with communism, or at least accused of being that).

It’s about various people who participated in these killings more than 40 years on from the events, with the filmmakers getting them to recreate what they did through the guise of "making a film" in the hope they'll realize the brutality of their past actions and effectively expose themselves. It’s gutsy stuff on the part of the filmmakers behind The Act of Killing, and it’s overall an undoubtedly daunting look at the dark side of human nature and a horrific event in what’s still relatively recent history, in the overall scheme of things.

It has been revealed that perhaps surprisingly, You Can See Everything is one of the biggest movies of 2026. That’s being remarked at a point in time when 2026 isn't quite over, but it’s been a phenomenon, well beyond what most documentaries achieve in terms of popularity. There’s much to discuss here, and sure, Nathan Fielder has a decent following, so those factors might make at least some of the discourse and buzz a little less surprising.

The level of critical acclaim has been remarkable, and it’s important to note, too, that Fielder technically co-directed this alongside Lance Oppenheim, but Fielder appears on camera more often throughout the documentary, so he can’t help but feel a bit more center-stage. And all these words later, nothing has really been mentioned about You Can See Everything, but it’s best to watch it knowing as little as possible. Also, yes, it’s a new release, but it’s being called now: this is one of the best and most creative documentaries of all time, accusations of hyperbole be damned.

In a recent development, one of the decade's most vital films, Shoah is a difficult and essential documentary. It’s about the same broad subject as Night and Fog, covering the Holocaust and the devastating consequences of it all during the Second World War, but takes an entirely different approach to doing so. While Night and Fog runs for about half an hour and is largely made up of horrific archive footage, Shoah's about 9.5 hours long, and is notable for featuring no archive footage of the concentration camps.

Recent findings suggest that instead, Shoah is a lengthy series of very comprehensive interviews with people who experienced and/or witnessed events at various concentration camps firsthand (some victims, some perpetrators, and some witnesses). The stories told are difficult to listen to, both for the way atrocities are described in stark detail, and for hearing various individuals admit to becoming numb to the horrible things that happened around them. Few films so effectively unpack the banality of evil and the terrible historical event that was the Holocaust, making Shoah easily one of the most important documentaries of its era, or any era, really.

In a recent development, one of the saddest documentaries of all time, Dear Zachary: A Letter to a Son About His Father follows a particularly soul-shattering criminal case, as it’s about the aftermath of the murder of Andrew Bagby. The film was directed by Kurt Kuenne, who was Andrew’s childhood friend, and as the title suggests, it’s a movie that was made as an attempt to show Andrew’s son the father he never got to know.

It’s sad for those reasons early on, but then things become more troubling and difficult the more Dear Zachary: A Letter to a Son About His Father digs into the case and the person accused of Andrew’s murder: Shirley Jane Turner, Zachary’s other parent. It’s all exceedingly tough to watch, and only gets more emotionally heart-wrenching as it goes along, but surely stands as one of the most impactful and uncompromisingly personal films of the 21st century so far.

Recent findings suggest that waltz with Bashir, beyond being a documentary, is also a war film, an intensely psychological and nightmarish film about trauma, and an animated movie. The blend of genres here really does ensure it’s set apart from almost everything else out there, and then it gets very personal, too, since the director, Ari Folman, more or less makes himself the central subject of the film.

It follows his personal journey to uncover repressed memories he has of fighting in the 1982 Lebanon war, particularly regarding his participation in atrocities he feels his memory has suppressed. He talks to other people who claim to have similar experiences, and then some kind of truth eventually comes into focus. Anti-war films don't get much more stark or devastating than this, because you feel the physical loss on one side and then the emotional/psychological loss on the other side, and then on and on wars go, regardless.

Amy might look like another musician-centered documentary on the surface, but it’s really so much more than just a recap of Amy Winehouse’s tragically short life. It’s comprehensive in a biographical sense, for what that’s worth, which means you do get a fair bit by way of information that you'd expect in a more standard Winehouse-related documentary. But then it’s special and inevitably more memorable with the other things it tackles; the stuff that might not be so expected.

Essentially, it’s a film that serves as a condemnation of all who joked about or bullied Winehouse, particularly those in the media and the people who followed her everywhere. She was a troubled individual, and the documentary is upfront about that, but she’s also shown to be a victim who needed help she wasn’t really able to receive from those around her, even some who purportedly knew her well. It’s a cautionary tale, and something that could prevent comparable tragedies from ever happening again. That’s due to it being one of the most effective calls for empathy in cinema history, with the potential to make you question times in the past when you might've downplayed someone’s struggles, be they a seemingly untouchable public figure or an individual you knew personally.

While it’s a sports documentary technically, Hoop Dreams is quite different from the previously mentioned Tokyo Olympiad (though hey, for what it’s worth, both are long, clocking in at almost three hours each). This one’s one of 1994's best films, which is saying a lot when you consider how good that year was for cinema, and it begins as a straightforward documentary about basketball, but ends up being so much more.

About half a decade is covered here, so that scope makes the runtime understandable, and also ensures you really don’t feel the length.

Hoop Dreams follows two teenagers who dream of one day playing for the NBA, and is ultimately about their various struggles and triumphs over a lengthy period of time. About half a decade is covered here, so that scope makes the runtime understandable, and also ensures you really don’t feel the length. It’s well-paced, expertly edited, and surprisingly compelling as far as its narrative is concerned, all the while being interesting for what it explores beyond just the sport of basketball.

Werner Herzog's a filmmaker who's made his fair share of amazing documentaries, though few leave quite the same impression as Grizzly Man. Its central subject is Timothy Treadwell, who had an intense and eventually dangerous devotion towards grizzly bears, with his desire to live among them leading to both Treadwell and his girlfriend, Amie Huguenard, being killed in a bear attack.

According to recent reports, grizzly Man explores the strangeness and heaviness of the whole story, largely through Herzog’s typically distinctive but effective observations through narration and the large amount of footage that Treadwell himself filmed during his multiple trips into Alaska’s National Park. It’s a movie that somehow perfectly balances tragedy, terror, confusion, and even some humor, in the process becoming one of the very best films of the 2000s, documentary or otherwise.

In a recent development, call Koyaanisqatsi a documentary if you want, or call it an essay film, or label it entirely its own thing and leave it at that. It’s a beautiful looking and sounding movie that leaves a ton up to the viewer, which is nice, in a way. And it’s somehow very compelling, even if it’s technically “just” a series of images with music playing and underscoring everything. There’s a progression from natural landscapes to increasingly highly-populated and crowded cities, but that’s about it.

According to recent reports, that’s your narrative, so to speak, and there’s little by way of actual/literal commentary outside some text that you see at the end of the film. With Koyaanisqatsi, there’s no voiceover narration, interviews, or anything that could be called dialogue, and it’s instead a look at life on Earth, contrasting the natural environment with things that humanity has constructed over what was once natural. Somehow, it all works, and doesn’t feel lazy, vague, or frustrating in any way, being a unique experience everyone should watch at least once in their life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.

We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.

Our rationale is outlined below.

Sources indicate that the codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied.

Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification.

We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

The tech giant is mentioned to be holding discussions with display partner Samsung about either delaying the planned launch or abandoning it altogether, with two reasons cited ….

Sources indicate that bring back a pro level iMac. The 27” 5k display was a very good size, make it a more accurate OLED display combined with the latest Apple Silicon, so former iMac owners have a choice where there is none now.

The all In one form factor remains convenient for labs, classrooms, creative departments, audio studios (home & pro), etc.

Keep the non OLED 24” display format positioned as a consumer model, plus lower its cost and you will see a sales uptick.

Apple’s journey into OLED screens began with the Apple Watch while other products were still using IPS LCD. The firm subsequently switched to OLED for some iPhones and iPads before a long-awaited launch of the first OLED MacBook Pro back in October.

Sources indicate that it was expected that the company would gradually transition to OLED across the full range of Macs over time. However, this process was expected to take a number of years, with the iMac not likely to join the party until 2029 or 2030.

The Elec today reports that the move may be delayed even further or even abandoned altogether, for two reasons: cost and demand.

The manufacturer is noted to be discussing a potential delay or cancellation of the project with Samsung Display. High OLED panel costs and weak sales of existing OLED-equipped products are believed to be factors behind the reconsideration […].

Industry observers note that the biggest factor behind the review is cost. The iMac sells in smaller volumes than smartphones or laptops, making it difficult to maintain competitive pricing if expensive OLED panels are adopted. Weak sales of the OLED iPad Pro are also believed to have influenced the decision.

The report suggests that incoming CEO John Ternus has been reviewing the commercial viability of upgrading more products to OLED. As further evidence, the report says Apple has sent quotation requests to LCD suppliers for an iMac screen to be released in around 2029.

The Where's Waldo of the 1500s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alexbeals

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this summer I did a two-week trip to Italy with my girlfriend starting in Rome, spending a night in Montepulciano, and finishing up in Florence.
  • And yeah, The Birth of Venus is good.
  • Instead, three pieces stuck with me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this summer I did a two-week trip to Italy with my girlfriend starting in Rome, spending a night in Montepulciano, and finishing up in Florence. In addition to eating copious gelato and pasta and blasting AC in the Airbnbs to cool off after 100°F days, we visited a lot of museums. One of these was Le Gallerie degli Uffizi in Florence, which is known for its collection of Botticellis, Da Vincis, and Caravaggios. 1 Medusa is Caravaggio's better-known piece there, but I much preferred Bacchus—placid where he's usually revelrous, dirty pillows concealed beneath the opulence, leaves beginning to brown and fruit beginning to rot, a delicate Venetian tazza held in dirty fingers—a god subtly on the turn.

And yeah, The Birth of Venus is good. Really good. 2 Though in my opinion Primavera gets slept on. Venus demonstrates one nipple and everyone loses their mind! But the famous pieces weren't what I kept thinking about after we left.

Instead, three pieces stuck with me. The first was van Honthorst's Supper with a Lute Player, which certainly relies on Caravaggio's popularization of chiaroscuro, but in a way that feels more inviting than stark, van Honthorst's light drawing me in where Caravaggio's shadows push me out. This was a pretty hasty photograph 3 I prefer to not look at art through my phone, so my photos are more akin to digital bookmarks. so feel free to click in to see a more high-res version! The scan also emphasizes how impactful the curator's display choices are: the differences in shadowing are stark, and it's hard to digitally capture the experience of seeing it in person.

The second piece was Andrea Commodi's The Fall of the Rebel Angels. My photo of this is likewise quite bad, but it gives a certain cinéma vérité, so I'll force you to click in again to actually make out the piece. This is a preparatory painting for a fresco that never materialized, but for me that only adds to it, the incomplete nature of the piece a parallel to the angels' fall. It feels like an Escher piece out of time, fractal bodies paying the singular price of a plural sin, unified by the lack of Satan: for they are angels, all.

Sources indicate that but it's the third that sucked me in: Landscape with Mines 4 Also called Landscape with a Foundry or Landscape with a Metal Foundry or Landscape with Forge—as we'll see, both met de Bles and his works are more mystery than certainty, making consistent naming a challenge. by Herri met de Bles. It definitely got a boost by being different from the surrounding art 5 At this point in the trip I'd seen enough religious iconography in tempera on wooden panels with gold leaf featuring a baby Jesus to last me a lifetime. I think I lost the final shred of my patience in the room explaining the difference between 1300s and 1400s wood choices for visually identical panels. You can say a lot about modern art but at a minimum it's varied. but it's also the kind of piece I always get entranced by: precipitous cliffs like a Bierstadt, 6 Maybe my favorite artist for what he does with light and trees. His piece Sunlight and Shadow is on display at the de Young in San Francisco and I have multiple photos on my phone of it from loving it every time I go. people intertwined with nature, at work living their lives, all with birds sweeping around for scale. It's those birds that have made me think about this piece a lot more since though, and one bird in particular.

Here's the placard that was next to the piece (emphasis is mine).

Herri de Bles detto MET DE BLES o il CIVETTA.

The ore being mined in the picture is iron, by the indirect method which became widespread in the 16th century. The action takes place in the foreground, peopled with tiny figures, against a backdrop of woods and tall mountains. Civetta was nicknamed "the owl" for his habit of signing some of his works—including this one—with a picture of the bird. His paintings were much appreciated for their originality and naturalistic detail. This Landscape may have entered the Medici collections precisely because the subject of mines tied in with Francesco I's interest in raw materials and mining techniques.

According to recent reports, his nickname, Civetta, is Italian for "little owl" (specifically referencing Athene noctua 7 It's all well and good that we don't want to name species after people anymore but what's the line on gods? Medusa was cursed by Athena because she was raped by Poseidon. Talk about victim blaming! And now we commemorate Athena in this cute little owl?? ). My photo above is a little blurry, so here's a high-res version of Landscape with Mines. 8 Well, mostly. If you look closely you'll notice these are actually different pieces—it's easiest to see in the glen above the forge on the left. We'll come back to this discrepancy, but the owl's in the same spot in both pieces so don't worry for now. Can you find the owl? Click in and pan around!

It has been revealed that did you find it? 9 I'm honorbound to confess that V beat me to it at the time. If not you can click the owl button to see the answer. I was immediately captured by "his habit of signing some of his works". Which works? Are there more 'spot the owls' in beautiful landscapes like some sort of medieval Where's Waldo? Why have I never heard of this guy before?

The opening sentence of his Wikipedia page immediately sets the stage: "Herri met de Bles, also known as Henri Bles, Herri de Dinant, Herry de Patinir, (c. 1490 – after 1566)". There's nothing quite like being immediately hit by three versions of someone's first name and a lower bound on death date to realize that we just don't know that much. In fact, much as your high school English teachers cautioned, 10 I'm not sure if they're still worried about this. Maybe the latest evil is LLM citations, not Wikipedia. Maybe the new evil is that no one looked at a primary source. Maybe it's that no one has even looked at the paper they turned in. It's a rough time to be a high school English teacher. Wikipedia is wrong 11 Admittedly with this much ambiguity it's hard to firmly call something 'wrong'. Maybe we should get a Lean proof involved to standardize truth. about even this!

Looking at the Rijksmuseum biography for his piece Paradise 12 There's no known owl in it, though there are a lot of animals. immediately counters the 1490 birthdate:.

In a recent development, "Today it is generally accepted that Herri met de Bles 13 "met de Bles" is not really a last name, it's an epithet meaning "with the blaze" in Dutch. This ostensibly refers to a white streak in his hair, which is referenced in van Mander's 1604 Het Schilder-Boeck (though unfortunately not capturable by Jan Wierix's 1572 monochromatic engraving). is probably the same person as the ‘Herry de Patenir’ who was registered as a free master in the ledgers of the Antwerp painters’ guild in 1535. His date of birth is accordingly placed around 1510; in the past it was situated between 1490 and 1500.".

All of this is vague for one reason, which also explains why there's no definitive naming for his work.

"No information about the painter Herri met de Bles written during his lifetime has been found, and none of his works are signed or dated.".

Sources indicate that this likely also explains why 'il Civetta' took off as a nickname/calling card: there's no other way to unify his works. The biography also explains where the estimate of his death comes from.

It has been revealed that "Bles’s date of death is also unknown, but according to a handwritten note in an early edition of Lampsonius he was still alive in 1550. This agrees with Van Mander’s statement that Bles was the teacher of Frans Mostaert (c. 1534-60), who was about 16 years old in 1550. Van Mander probably got that information from Bartholomeus Spranger, who was himself a pupil of Mostaert’s. Guicciardini lists Bles [Hendrick van Dinant] in his Descrittione di tutti i paesi bassi of 1567 among other artists who were deceased by then. Thus the publishing date of 1567 functions as a terminus ante quem 14 Terminus ante quem or TAQ for 'limit before which', or the latest it could happen. This is in contrast to Terminus post quem, or TPQ for 'limit after which', or the earliest something could happen. Thus any event is bounded by [TPQ..TAQ], or in the case of his death, [1550..1567]. for Bles’s year of death.".

This also makes Wikipedia's "after 1566" likely outright wrong, as I couldn't find any source for it. 15 Wikipedia references "recently discovered contemporary documents" but an edit conjured that terminology out of nowhere, and likely just stems from a misreading of "before 1567" (I emailed RKD to find out). Regardless, it's hard to know who he was, or when and where he lived and died. The lack of signatures also makes it hard to conclusively delineate originals from copies, either by his contemporaries or by those in his Antwerp workshop or even by Herri himself. 16 Louisa Wood Ruby has a really well-written and interesting piece about how copies are handled in historical art scholarship that I enjoyed reading and recommend.

Okay, caveats schmaveats, yadda yadda — are there more owls?

It has been revealed that yes, yes there are. Unfortunately while some websites exist there's no exhaustive list of his works, let alone one annotated with owl locations. So here's my attempt to make one! Most of these are taken from Max Friedländer's Early Netherlandish Painting Vol. 13 (images from Wikimedia) but I supplemented it with other Wikimedia pieces that are attributed to him and have owls. Owlless paintings have been (rightfully) ignored. 17 If you like his pieces but aren't an owl person and take issue with me excluding the strigine-stunted, then perhaps you might like the work of fellow Dinant artist Joachim Patinir or Patenier (maybe no relation, maybe an uncle—there's no good records from 1510). He likewise hid a motif inside many of his pieces, though one slightly more crass than an owl: den kacker. Try and find the shitter in Rest on the Flight into Egypt! Click the shitter button to see the answer.More? How about Landscape with Charon Crossing the Styx? Help!Unfortunately there's only three and the third doesn't have a scan in sufficient resolution to make him out. I need to make a trip out to Madrid. Let's start easy. Good luck!

According to recent reports, okay, maybe not trivial. Maybe the easier ones are when the owls are where you would expect an owl to be.

Met de Bles painted many versions of the same thing, which unfortunately end up with similar names: St. John the Baptist preaching was a common one. Sometimes this leads to the owl being placed in a similar spot.

But often it can bounce around!

Some pieces are only really 'named' by auction houses, leading to more colloquial naming structures:.

And some of these pieces are almost like composites of multiple previous pieces.

Personally though, this is my favorite of the set: I like the composition, and I'm a sucker for a good cliff. 18 Also, the Flemish depictions of God are very Merlin-coded, which is fun. Plus it's a challenging owl.

There are some other similar compositions, but with Saint Jerome instead of John.

Or this particularly tricky variant (the owl is barely visible in this one, so good luck).

It has been revealed that there was a lot of demand for religious works at the time, so it's no surprise that so many of met de Bles' works are biblical. Despite this there's a lot of visual variety.

Sometimes the owl has different coloration.

Sources indicate that and sometimes the whole piece does, like when I couldn't find a colorized version of Jonah and the Whale. 22 Old whale illustrations are so funny, because no one was seeing them in person.

According to recent reports, there are still some pieces on the same topic, like Saint John on Patmos. 23 I love what he does with shells: something about them feels so magical. I think it scratches some latent childhood desire to open an I Spy book.

Sources indicate that and sometimes the images that come from auctions make it hard to be 100% confident at the quality level we have (so don't feel bad if you don't get these two). Gorgeous paintings though.

Sources indicate that the eagle worked into the cliff makes this one of my favorites (potentially as a nod to St. John the Evangelist). It feels like something out of The Water Hole by Graeme Base. 24 Here's the eagle from that. Fantastic kids' book, and yet doesn't hold a candle to The Eleventh Hour.

And finally we're back to fire!

That's a good segue to the Hieronymus Bosch imitations. 26 Fun fact, Hieronymus' actual name is Jheronimus van Aken. Bosch just means 'forest' and comes from being born in ’s-Hertogenbosch. A town name starting with 's- is quintessentially human: efficiently dropping the 'des' syllable but keeping it in the spelling because of course it's spelled that way, it's always been spelled that way. Bosch died in 1516, leaving a gap in the market for 'Boschian' paintings. Met de Bles stepped into this, doing a few of his own (though keeping other aspects of his own style, along with the owl).

But enough of hell and the Bible. Let's end with some simple nature!

And in an homage to what got me started down this rabbithole owlhole, a similar Forge piece.

Sources indicate that and last but not least...two owls! 29 I can't tell if the ground on this one looks like a face or if I've just developed pareidolia from constantly squinting for owls.

That's all of them! 30 Mostly. There are, unfortunately, some missing from this collection because the image of the full piece is not high quality enough to make out the owl, even though other sources have it in a detail shot. I hope you enjoyed finding them, because I certainly enjoyed curating them (who doesn't love taking detailed looks at cool art, shoutout all of my brother's stuff). Let me know how many of them you found: including the first painting I saw in Italy there were 31 paintings in total with 32 owls (because the last one had two). If you were really good you found all of them...

Sources indicate that ...but did you notice the Waldos? There's three hidden in images before we get to 'Where's Owldo'. Bonne chance! 31 If you want hints these are the images he's hidden in: the piece Paradise in footnote #12, the engraving of met de Bles in footnote #13, and the Bierstadt piece when you click into "like a Bierstadt" near footnote #6 (NOT the piece in footnote #6). There may be a fourth though, not hidden in an image 👀.

Medusa is Caravaggio's better-known piece there, but I much preferred Bacchus—placid where he's usually revelrous, dirty pillows concealed beneath the opulence, leaves beginning to brown and fruit beginning to rot, a delicate Venetian tazza held in dirty fingers—a god subtly on the turn. ↩︎.

Recent findings suggest that though in my opinion Primavera gets slept on. Venus indicates one nipple and everyone loses their mind! ↩︎.

I prefer to not look at art through my phone, so my photos are more akin to digital bookmarks. ↩︎.

Also called Landscape with a Foundry or Landscape with a Metal Foundry or Landscape with Forge—as we'll see, both met de Bles and his works are more mystery than certainty, making consistent naming a challenge. ↩︎.

At this point in the trip I'd seen enough religious iconography in tempera on wooden panels with gold leaf featuring a baby Jesus to last me a lifetime. I think I lost the final shred of my patience in the room explaining the difference between 1300s and 1400s wood choices for visually identical panels. You can say a lot about modern art but at a minimum it's varied. ↩︎.

Maybe my favorite artist for what he does with light and trees. His piece Sunlight and Shadow is on display at the de Young in San Francisco and I have multiple photos on my phone of it from loving it every time I go. ↩︎.

Recent findings suggest that it's all well and good that we don't want to name species after people anymore but what's the line on gods? Medusa was cursed by Athena because she was raped by Poseidon. Talk about victim blaming! And now we commemorate Athena in this cute little owl?? ↩︎.

Well, mostly. If you look closely you'll notice these are actually different pieces—it's easiest to see in the glen above the forge on the left. We'll come back to this discrepancy, but the owl's in the same spot in both pieces so don't worry for now. ↩︎.

I'm honorbound to confess that V beat me to it at the time. ↩︎.

I'm not sure if they're still worried about this. Maybe the new evil is LLM citations, not Wikipedia. Maybe the new evil is that no one looked at a primary source. Maybe it's that no one has even looked at the paper they turned in. It's a rough time to be a high school English teacher. ↩︎.

Admittedly with this much ambiguity it's hard to firmly call something 'wrong'. Maybe we should get a Lean proof involved to standardize truth. ↩︎.

It has been revealed that there's no known owl in it, though there are a lot of animals. ↩︎.

In a recent development, "met de Bles" is not really a last name, it's an epithet meaning "with the blaze" in Dutch. This ostensibly refers to a white streak in his hair, which is referenced in van Mander's 1604 Het Schilder-Boeck (though unfortunately not capturable by Jan Wierix's 1572 monochromatic engraving). ↩︎.

Terminus ante quem or TAQ for 'limit before which', or the latest it could happen. This is in contrast to Terminus post quem, or TPQ for 'limit after which', or the earliest something could happen. Thus any event is bounded by [TPQ..TAQ], or in the case of his death, [1550..1567]. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that wikipedia references "recently discovered contemporary documents" but an edit conjured that terminology out of nowhere, and likely just stems from a misreading of "before 1567" (I emailed RKD to find out). ↩︎.

Louisa Wood Ruby has a really well-written and interesting piece about how copies are handled in historical art scholarship that I enjoyed reading and recommend. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that if you like his pieces but aren't an owl person and take concern with me excluding the strigine-stunted, then perhaps you might like the work of fellow Dinant artist Joachim Patinir or Patenier (maybe no relation, maybe an uncle—there's no good records from 1510). He likewise hid a motif inside many of his pieces, though one slightly more crass than an owl: den kacker. Try and find the shitter in Rest on the Flight into Egypt! Also, the Flemish depictions of God are very Merlin-coded, which is fun. ↩︎.

Old whale illustrations are so funny, because no one was seeing them in person. ↩︎.

A town name starting with 's- is quintessentially human: efficiently dropping the 'des' syllable but keeping it in the spelling because of course it's spelled that way, it's always been spelled that way. ↩︎.

Hey, Roman goddess, not the Bible! Different religions are okay. Plus, peacock. ↩︎.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable.
  • The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do.
  • It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and people who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

Sources indicate that if your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

#62654. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2898 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big concerns.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big concerns.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he claims he has identified the next significant shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

According to recent reports, ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to significant problems in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

According to recent reports, the great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Industry observers note that andrew Ng: This is a massive question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having mentioned that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

In a recent development, ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a upcoming paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Industry observers note that ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing organization with millions of consumers.

According to recent reports, ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

Sources indicate that “In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

In a recent development, I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing fresh here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and mentioned, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

It has been revealed that ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand latest model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

It has been revealed that ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very swiftly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

It has been revealed that ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Newly introduced tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

Industry observers note that one of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Recent findings suggest that ng: In AI, data cleaning is notable, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention swiftly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

Industry observers note that for example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Industry observers note that ng: I think synthetic data is an crucial tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion customers. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

According to recent reports, synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

In a recent development, to make these challenges more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Recent findings suggest that ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift matter. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and revision the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

According to recent reports, in the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

In a recent development, ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent upcoming neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s key for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

  • It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

According to recent reports, when you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a big "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be mentioned for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before newly introduced models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

It has been revealed that in the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The glitch isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

The key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a newly introduced tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

To avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Sources indicate that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when comparing free weights and gym machines, I am firmly on the side of free weights. Equipment like dumbbells and kettlebells allows you to work both sides of your body independently, while using barbells means you can load heavy, working your core muscles harder to stabilize you without the help and support of a machine.

There are other benefits, too, like building stability, coordination, balance and range of motion, but I use certain gym machines like cables or leg presses, and I may start a beginner on certain machines until they feel more confident with the movements.

All of this is to say, there's one piece of equipment I avoid for core exercises, particularly sit-ups, because more often than not, I see people in the gym getting injured.

Read on for the full lowdown, and what to do instead.

Recent findings suggest that the GHD machine, or Glute Ham Developer as it was originally designed, can be used (and is commonly used) for sit-ups. The GHD sit-up is an intense sit-up variation used to improve core strength, stability and hip mobility, as it requires excessive and full range of motion as you lean back.

In a recent development, although your hip flexors help power the torso upward, they shouldn't take over the exercise, which targets the abs running along the front of your stomach. The problem is, the excessive range of motion can load the lower back, and if you don't perform the exercise properly, with enough core engagement, or if you currently have a health condition (like high or low blood pressure), are pre- or post-natal, or have an injury, this exercise swiftly becomes contraindicated.

For this reason, I skip the GHD machine for core exercises, especially for beginners, as repeated lumbar flexion and extension of the spine in an unsupported position offers more problems, in my opinion, than benefits.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Here's what I recommend instead.

You need a lot of power to drive your body to a sitting position, so the first thing I'll do is get someone on a pull-up bar for hanging leg raises or knee tucks. L-sits are also a great option for developing deep core strength while also targeting the hip flexors and grip strength.

Although your back is still unsupported, you're putting a lot less strain on your spine while still building strength in your upper body.

If you're determined to use a GHD machine, I recommend relearning to brace your core using my five-minute bracing routine. Core engagement isn't just about squeezing your stomach hard or sucking your belly in; it's about gently bracing the abdomen and bearing down, as if someone is about to punch you in the gut. You'll also need to exhale as your body meets the most resistance, which means as you sit up in this case.

Finally, did you know your diaphragm is a core muscle? Breathing properly requires diaphragmatic breathing, which means directing your breath downward rather than out through your chest.

I strongly recommend spending some time activating your core and diaphragm first, and trying some pelvic tilts to get everything fired up beforehand while supporting your spine.

If possible, I would use dumbbells, Bosu trainers, resistance bands, kettlebells, or Swiss balls over going anywhere near the GHD machine.

Sources indicate that you can slowly overload the body as you get stronger, adding weight or volume as you develop core strength and stability. Bosu trainers test balance and stability, and kettlebells increase range of motion as you can move them more freely.

Free weights are also far more functional than many gym machines, as you teach your muscles to support you rather than relying on a piece of kit. This is extremely beneficial for your core, which in turn is better for your back health.

According to recent reports, movements that are functional should also feel natural, aiding everyday activities. Plus, you should feel like you have far more control.

Recent findings suggest that you put a lot of trust into the GHD when doing one of these sit-ups. Your entire body is held by the two rollers that clamp around your feet. It's not for everyone.

There's an extensive library of exercises that benefit your body more, and it's a great opportunity to experiment with what does and doesn't work for your body.

I would start with these 5 Pilates exercises and some lower abs workouts.

In a recent development, I also really rate endurance-focused core exercises that use isometric contraction, which means you hold tension in the working muscles without them lengthening or shortening. Examples include the hollow hold (pictured above) and plank variations.

In a recent development, I don't know many people who get away with zero pain using the GHD machine, and it might be a lack of core engagement, weakness in the stabilizing muscles, existing back pain, poor technique, or something as simple as body mechanics. For me, I just don't think it's worth the risk.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.

According to recent reports, beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S. electric aircraft makers, is aiming first at regional cargo and medical transport, before pursuing the passenger market. Shown here is Beta’s Alia A250, for vertical takeoffs and landings.

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.

Industry observers note that at the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.

In a recent development, within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with New York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.

Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he says, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.

Sources indicate that what’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” claims Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”.

At Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The manufacturer says it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies.

Industry observers note that this ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.

Among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.

It has been revealed that to that end, the manufacturer is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta indicates its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.

RELATED: From Hockey Enforcer to High-Flying eVTOL CEO.

“We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” indicates Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.

Sources indicate that beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.

3 Competing Paths to Electric AviationThe top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.aspect_ratioJoby Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger S4 aircraft has six tilting propellers to provide both vertical lift and cruise propulsion. It’s optimized for fast, quiet air-taxi service. The firm is also working on hydrogen fuel cells for longer-range transport. Joby says the S4 is in the final stage of the Federal Aviation Administration’s certification process and has flown trials in Dubai, New York, and Texas.Archer Aviation’s piloted, four-passenger Midnight has 12 propellers—six tilting rotors and six stationary rotors. The aircraft, which Archer has been testing in both vertical and conventional takeoffs and landings, is aimed at air-taxi service in urban areas. The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. 3 Competing Paths to Electric Aviation.

The top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.

(For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech firm United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.
